items.title: Vera Delivers the Best of Both Worlds: Highest Throughput and Fastest Agents
items.description: AI agents do more than generate answers. items.content: AI agents do more than generate answers. They search for information, query databases, write and test code and take action. Each of those steps relies on a CPU, with agents moving between GPU reasoning and CPU execution throughout a task. As businesses put more agents to work, AI factories need CPUs that can execute those steps quickly and support many agents at once, all within the limits of available power. What this means: AI infrastructure providers need to support more agents without making each one wait longer to get work done. And critically, AI factories are power limited. This means operators need to choose infrastructure that maximizes the work done for every watt. Why it matters: NVIDIA Vera delivers both fast agent performance and high capacity per watt within a single CPU. That gives providers one CPU for a range of agent workloads, rather than having to mix and match fast and dense x86 parts to balance speed and capacity. The data that proves it: In a 100-megawatt data center comparison, NVIDIA found that a single Vera CPU performs better than the fastest x86 CPU and the most energy-efficient x86 CPU. Vera delivers industry-leading agent speed while enabling 1.6x more agents per watt versus the fastest x86 CPU. Vera delivers 2x faster agent speed with leading energy efficiency compared with the most energy-efficient x86 CPU. Partners are already putting Vera to work. Early adopters see the same exceptional performance in production-style tests: Perplexity: Ran agentic coding tasks 1.5x faster with Vera than on traditional CPUs. Perplexity plans to deploy Vera in an upcoming production system. DeepInfra: Delivered up to 2.2x speed of the best x86 processor on agentic orchestration for its production agent workload, achieving the fastest of the four architectures tested. ClickHouse: Its standard binary, with no Vera-specific tuning, scaled near-linearly across 176 cores and topped the ClickBench hardware leaderboard. DuckLabs: Achieved about 1.5x the median TPC-H SF1000 performance of an Intel Xeon 6 baseline. Daytona: Brought 1,000 agent sandboxes online in 10.8 seconds, and achieved 12.7 completed jobs per second at 2,000 concurrent sandboxes, using Vera versus 88.4 seconds with x86. Modal: Achieved up to 2x sandbox throughput per core versus comparable x86 hardware, with gains that grow under heavy load. Learn more about the NVIDIA Vera CPU.
items.author: Hannah Coutand
items.titleZh: Vera 实现两全其美：最高吞吐量与最快智能体
items.descriptionZh:
AI智能体并不只是生成答案，它还会检索信息、查询数据库、编写和测试代码并执行动作。上述每一步都依赖CPU，智能体在一个任务中会反复在GPU推理与CPU执行之间切换。随着企业部署越来越多智能体，AI工厂需要能够快速执行这些步骤、同时支持大量智能体并发运行的CPU，并且必须在可用功耗约束内完成。这意味着AI基础设施提供商既要提升智能体并发容量，又不能显著拉长单个智能体的等待时间；更关键的是，AI工厂受功耗限制，运营方需要选择“每瓦完成最多工作”的基础设施。

NVIDIA Vera CPU的定位正是同时提供快速的智能体性能和较高的每瓦容量。NVIDIA指出，Vera在单颗CPU内兼顾智能体执行速度与能效容量，使提供商可以用一款CPU覆盖多种智能体负载，而不必在“更快的x86”和“更密集的x86”之间混搭，以平衡速度与容量。

在NVIDIA公布的一项100兆瓦数据中心对比中，单颗Vera CPU的表现优于最快的x86 CPU和最节能的x86 CPU。具体来看，Vera在提供业界领先智能体速度的同时，相比最快x86 CPU可实现每瓦1.6倍的智能体数量；相比最节能x86 CPU，Vera在保持领先能效的同时实现2倍更快的智能体速度。

合作伙伴的生产型测试也展示了Vera在智能体负载中的表现：Perplexity在智能体编程任务中使用Vera比传统CPU快1.5倍，并计划在即将上线的生产系统中部署Vera；DeepInfra在其生产智能体负载的智能体编排任务中，使用Vera达到最佳x86处理器最高2.2倍的速度，在测试的四种架构中最快；ClickHouse使用未针对Vera做专门调优的标准二进制版本，在176核上接近线性扩展，并登上ClickBench硬件排行榜首位；DuckLabs达到Intel Xeon 6基线约1.5倍的中位TPC-H SF1000性能；Daytona使用Vera在10.8秒内上线1000个智能体沙箱，并在2000个并发沙箱下实现每秒12.7个完成任务，而x86对应上线时间为88.4秒；Modal相比同类x86硬件实现每核最高2倍沙箱吞吐量，且在高负载下增益进一步扩大。

整体来看，Vera面向的是智能体规模化运行后的CPU瓶颈：智能体编排、工具调用、代码执行、数据库查询和沙箱并发等任务需要低延迟与高并发并存。Vera通过单颗CPU平衡速度与每瓦容量，旨在帮助AI工厂在功耗受限条件下提升智能体吞吐和响应速度，减少基础设施选型复杂度，并覆盖编程智能体、生产级智能体编排、数据库分析、沙箱环境和重负载并发等多种应用场景。

items.title: India targets creating homegrown GPUs within 2 years and plans to commercialize indigenous SHAKTI and VEGA processors
items.description: MeitY Secretary S. Krishnan says India plans to develop its own GPU under Semiconductor Mission 2.0, with a target of approximately two years. The country is also looking to commercialize its SHAKTI and VEGA RISC-V processors, expand domestic server production, and attract more semiconductor investment. Krishnan sees the AI boom as a potential repeat of the Y2K-era opportunity that helped India's IT services industry grow
items.content: Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 5 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter India wants to develop its own graphics processing unit (GPU) within the next two years as the country steps up efforts to build a domestic semiconductor industry and reduce its dependence on foreign chip suppliers, reports ETGovernment. The target was outlined by S.Krishnan, secretary of India's Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), in a November 4 interview. "Under India Semiconductor Mission 2.0, we intend to target the development of an indigenous GPU chip. We should have a GPU chip of our own. This will not happen overnight. It is a project that will require approximately 24 months, and we intend to work towards that objective," Krishnan said.The proposed GPU is part of a wider plan to establish an Indian hardware and software ecosystem, with Krishnan describing five layers needed to support AI development. These include: energy, accelerator chips, computing infrastructure and servers, AI models and applications. Indian companies such as VVDN, Kaynes and Avalon are already manufacturing servers, while the Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (C-DAC) has developed its Rudra server range, whose systems are designed to support AI workloads, after which the government transfers the technology to local manufacturers. Krishnan also sees AI as a potential repeat of the opportunity India's IT industry experienced during the Y2K (the year 2000 bug) transition. "AI could create a similar opportunity, although the nature of the work will be different," he said.The comparison is big for a country whose IT-enabled service sector employs about 6 million people. A NITI Aayog paper estimates that roughly two million existing jobs could become redundant as AI adoption changes the industry, but around 4 million more jobs could emerge. Krishnan argues that Indian companies could benefit from helping businesses worldwide integrate into their AI operations, just as they benefited from the demand for software services around the turn of the century.Latest Videos FromTom's HardwareWatch full video here: The country has already attracted major interest with ASML, partnering with Tata Electronics to equip India's first commercial semiconductor fabrication facility in Dholera, Gujarat. The planned facility is expected to use 300mm wafers and eventually reach a capacity of 50,000 wafers per month. Intel also announced a strategic partnership with Tata Group covering semiconductor manufacturing and packaging for the Indian market. However, the proposed GPU remains an early-stage target. Krishnan did not identify a manufacturer, chip supplier, or builder for the project. India is also looking to bring its own homegrown SHAKTI and VEGA processors to commercial markets. Both are based on the open-source RISC-V architecture, allowing local developers to build processors without relying on proprietary CPU designs. Notably, these are CPU designs, separate from the GPUs now being targeted by MeitY.That said, it is not the first time India has attempted to build its own GPU production unit. In 2019, India's IT Madras released a software development kit that allowed developers to begin building applications before the processors were commercialized. The project included several processor classes aimed at different markets, from embedded devices and micro-controllers to workstations and server workloads. The effort has continued since then, with the Aries 3.0 development board, which uses the C-DAC’s VEGA ET301 processor, being introduced in 2024. The 32-bit chip runs up to 100MHz and includes 26KB of SRAM and is intended for relatively simple applications such as sensors, wearables, and Internet of Things devices, rather than desktop PCs or graphics-intensive workloads. You may like China's homegrown AI accelerators to supply 90% of the country's domestic market, analysts suggest ‘This is how AI should be used’ — OpenAI head of hardware breaks down the AI-assisted design of its Jalapeño ASIC Russian chipmakers demo homegrown RISC-V and Arm chips with retro games However, there are signs that the SHAKTI and VEGA platforms are nodding beyond development boards and into practical applications. At the September 26 SEMICOM India event, the government highlighted projects using the processors, including an autonomous water-cleaning robot around SHAKTI and a digital telescope using VEGA. Another VEGA-based project was designed to monitor forest environments. The government's Design -linked Incentive (DLI) program is already supporting more of that work. MeiyT says 24 companies received assistance under the scheme, and subsequently raised venture capital or other private investment. Their projects include microcontrollers, drone flight controllers, smart meter chips and CCTV cameras.India's semiconductor market is currently valued at just about $50billion and is expected to approach 100 billion by 2030, according to a report by the India Electronics and Semiconductor Association (IESA). The government wants local companies to capture more of that growth domestically rather than remain dependent on imported components.Stay On the Cutting Edge: Get the Tom's Hardware NewsletterGet Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.Contact me with news and offers from other Future brandsReceive email from us on behalf of our trusted partners or sponsors Follow Tom's Hardware on Google News, or add us as a preferred source, to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds.
items.author: Newton Gitonga
items.titleZh: 印度目标两年内打造国产GPU，并计划将本土SHAKTI和VEGA处理器商业化
items.descriptionZh:
印度电子和信息技术部（MeitY）秘书S·克里希南在11月4日接受采访时表示，印度计划在未来约24个月内开发出自己的图形处理器（GPU），作为“印度半导体使命2.0”下的重要目标。这标志着印度在加快构建本土半导体产业、减少对外国芯片供应商依赖方面迈出新的一步。不过，该GPU项目仍处于早期阶段，克里希南没有说明由哪家企业制造、由谁供应芯片或承建该项目。

克里希南将这一目标放在更广泛的印度软硬件生态建设框架中。他提出支撑人工智能发展需要五个层次：能源、加速器芯片、计算基础设施和服务器、AI模型以及应用。印度企业VVDN、Kaynes和Avalon已在制造服务器，印度高级计算发展中心（C-DAC）则开发了Rudra服务器系列，相关系统面向AI工作负载设计，之后由政府将技术转让给本地制造商。克里希南还把AI视为印度可能重现“千年虫”时期IT产业机遇的领域，认为AI可能创造类似机会，尽管工作性质会有所不同。

这一类比对印度意义重大。印度IT服务产业雇用了约600万人。印度国家转型委员会（NITI Aayog）的一份文件估计，随着AI应用改变行业，约200万个现有岗位可能变得冗余，但也可能新增约400万个岗位。克里希南认为，印度企业可以帮助全球企业将其业务融入AI运营，就像本世纪初它们受益于软件服务需求一样。

在半导体制造方面，印度已吸引重要国际企业关注。ASML与塔塔电子合作，为印度首个商业半导体晶圆厂提供设备，该厂位于古吉拉特邦多莱拉，预计使用300毫米晶圆，最终达到每月5万片晶圆产能。英特尔也宣布与塔塔集团建立战略合作，覆盖面向印度市场的半导体制造和封装。但拟议中的本土GPU仍是早期目标，尚未明确制造方、芯片供应商或建设方。

印度还在推动本土SHAKTI和VEGA处理器进入商用市场。两者均基于开源RISC-V架构，使本地开发者无需依赖专有CPU设计即可构建处理器。不过，这些属于CPU设计，与MeitY当前瞄准的GPU是不同类别。印度此前也曾尝试建设自己的GPU生产单元。2019年，印度理工学院马德拉斯分校发布软件开发工具包，让开发者在处理器商业化前开始构建应用；项目包含面向嵌入式设备、微控制器、工作站和服务器等不同市场的处理器类别。此后工作持续进行，2024年推出了使用C-DAC VEGA ET301处理器的Aries 3.0开发板。该32位芯片最高运行频率100MHz，包含26KB SRAM，面向传感器、可穿戴设备和物联网设备等相对简单的应用，而非桌面PC或图形密集型工作负载。

不过，SHAKTI和VEGA平台正显示出从开发板走向实际应用的迹象。在9月26日SEMICON India活动上，政府展示了使用这些处理器的项目，包括基于SHAKTI的自主水面清洁机器人、使用VEGA的数字望远镜，以及另一个基于VEGA的森林环境监测项目。政府的“设计关联激励”（DLI）计划已支持更多此类工作。MeitY称，已有24家公司在计划下获得援助，并随后筹集了风险投资或其他私人投资，项目包括微控制器、无人机飞控、智能电表芯片和闭路电视摄像头。

据印度电子和半导体协会（IESA）报告，印度半导体市场目前价值约500亿美元，预计到2030年接近1000亿美元。印度政府希望本土企业更多地在国内捕获这一增长，而不是继续依赖进口零部件。

items.title: ‘Total repudiation’: The blue wave is about to hit AI
items.description:

items.content: On Tuesday night, Democrats made history as they took control of the House and the Senate, and a blue wave swept through traditionally red and swing states — with the nation’s first Black woman governor elected in Georgia, the country’s first Native American woman governor elected in New Mexico, and a Maine Senator ceding to a Democrat after 30 years in office. In these and other campaigns, one theme kept coming up: holding AI companies accountable to the American people. Now, the AI industry is left considering the prospect of regulation, data center construction slowdowns, and more.Publicly, most major AI company CEOs have remained silent. OpenAI and Anthropic did not provide comments to The Verge; Elon Musk’s call on X to vote “red” for the midterms — the SpaceX CEO had spent close to $450 million backing Republican campaigns for the election — vanished after results poured in.Privately, CEOs have discussed significant compute capacity constraints for their companies after Tuesday’s results, particularly OpenAI, per The Wall Street Journal. Meta’s platforms president, Dina Powell McCormick, says many are considering moving data center construction abroad. AI executives are reportedly privately nervous about the results but may also be able to blame them for not delivering as much revenue to investors. Many of the incoming leaders have promised to drag CEOs to testify. On X, a popular post by former X product lead Nikita Bier warned that “This is going to be like the Nuremberg Trials but for AI researchers.” (On Tuesday night, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman did post about how “people should always be in control of the future,” but he spent other parts of the evening talking about RAM.)Tuesday’s results were a “total repudiation” of the AI field, says Wes McEnany, the former Deputy Labor Policy Director of the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, & Pensions, who now works with the nonprofit Future of Life Institute. He said that AI touches “every aspect of people’s lives,” whether they’re applying for jobs, using social media, or even paying electricity bills while living near a data center, and that they’re tired of not having “any agency in that conversation.”The bipartisan backlash against data center construction is the most tangible manifestation of that backlash. It’s going to be unquestionably more difficult to build them across the country, after 43 out of 44 local data center moratoria on Tuesday’s ballots passed, sending a clear message to AI companies. In Texas, the fastest-growing data center buildout area and a key battleground state, governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has said she plans to “issue a moratorium — a ban — on all data center approvals until laws can be passed by the legislature to protect Texans.” Similar promises have been made in a handful of other key states.“Data centers were clearly on the ballot,” said Guru Sethupathy, GM of AI governance at Optro.In recent months, there’s been an increasing number of protests and collective bipartisan action to battle data centers being built in a wide range of states. Residents are concerned about noise pollution, electricity bill rate hikes, and more. When NBC News polled voters on Tuesday, 76 percent opposed data centers in their communities.“The data center backlash is one of the most bipartisan political issues I’ve ever seen,” Shaunna Thomas, co-founder and director of the Guardrails Alliance, a Super PAC pushing for AI regulation.“Data centers are an entry point to looking at this broader corporate accountability lens of, ‘My bill is going up, why?’” said Kyle Jacobs-Morse, deputy executive director at The Tech Oversight Project, a nonprofit tech industry watchdog. “People found that it was big tech companies that were the culprit.” He added that particularly in the gubernatorial races in Texas, Georgia, and Ohio, Democratic campaigns prioritized potential local issues stemming from data centers, including “spillover costs” for local residents, communities, and state governments.“I do think we’ll hear more questions about who benefits from and who pays for AI, especially as it pertains to infrastructure, but what I’m more curious about is what changes we can expect around regulation,” said François Ajenstat, CEO and founder of Golden Analytics.Experts say the midterm results have likely ended Trump and congressional Republicans’ repeated attempts to bar state-level AI restrictions. Thomas considers the idea “completely dead,” while McEnany said “any member who votes to wipe out state AI laws is going to be looking for a job in the next [election].” Jacobs-Morse expects to generally see more “tech accountability bills.”OpenAI recently began calling its data centers “compute campuses,” and President Trump in September attempted to change the name of AI as a technology to “super intelligence.” But midterm results suggest that a significant portion of American voters aren’t buying the rebranding efforts.“I don’t think it was working, and I think the prospect of it working is extremely low after the election,” Thomas said.“The Trump idiosyncrasies around some of this stuff… they did not play well at the ballot box,” Jacobs-Morse said.But some in and around the tech industry are taking the news more positively than others. One X user wrote that “we’re *maybe* back to being a rational, steady hand as a country and can really lead,” while others wrote that the recent results could be good for preventing an AI bubble burst. Katie Barr, CEO of Glen Echo Group and a partner at Orchestra, said she wouldn’t “over-read” the results as an overwhelming tech rejection but rather a reckoning on “affordability, jobs, safety, and whether people have a say in what’s happening in their communities and their lives.”Analysts at Yorkville Ives & Co. wrote in a note that though tech investors should prepare for “major hurdles for AI and tech legislation” and a slowdown of the planned construction of up to 1,000 data centers across the country, there could be a “slight positive” in that it could help avoid a bubble and slow capital fundraising flooding the market.There will also likely be a reckoning on AI safety. Sen. Mark Warner (D-Va.) was reelected after campaigning for AI safety policy, and in a victory speech Tuesday by Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), Ossoff said, “The titans of Silicon Valley dig bunkers for themselves and warn that the artificial intelligence they’re creating risks human extinction.” Some AI safety legislation is already being considered, like the bill to “ban superintelligence” introduced in September by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas).President Trump has dismissed the idea of a safety crisis in AI as a “hoax,” writing on social media that “the only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT.” After the midterms, however, Republican lawmakers will need to decide whether to fall in line or negotiate with Democrats on safety-focused policy measures. Either way, Adam Kovacevich, founder and CEO of Chamber of Progress, a pro-tech industry advocacy group, said he expects AI safety legislation to continue to happen in blue states.“There’s a lot of open questions about where democrats go next on tech policy. Do we revert to the Biden era war on tech, the Obama era tech honeymoon, or something in between?” Kovacevich said.
items.author: Hayden Field
items.titleZh: “彻底否定”：蓝色浪潮即将冲击人工智能
items.descriptionZh:
周二晚美国中期选举中，民主党赢得众议院和参议院控制权，一场“蓝色浪潮”席卷传统红州和摇摆州：佐治亚州选出全美首位黑人女性州长，新墨西哥州选出首位原住民女性州长，缅因州一位任职30年的参议员将席位让给民主党人。在这些及其他竞选活动中，一个反复出现的主题是追究AI公司对美国人民的责任。如今，AI行业开始面对监管收紧、数据中心建设放缓等前景。

公开层面，多数大型AI公司CEO保持沉默。OpenAI和Anthropic未向The Verge置评；埃隆·马斯克曾在X上呼吁中期选举投“红色”，其支持共和党竞选活动的支出接近4.5亿美元，但选举结果出炉后该帖文消失。私下里，据《华尔街日报》报道，CEO们已讨论周二结果后公司面临的显著算力容量限制，尤其是OpenAI。Meta平台总裁Dina Powell McCormick表示，许多公司正考虑将数据中心建设转向海外。AI高管据称对选举结果私下感到紧张，但也可能借此解释为何未能向投资者交付足够收入。许多即将上任的领导人已承诺传唤CEO作证。X上前产品负责人Nikita Bier的一则热门帖文警告称，“这将像纽伦堡审判，但对象是AI研究者。”周二晚，OpenAI CEO Sam Altman发帖称“人们应始终掌控未来”，但当晚其他时间他在谈论RAM。

前参议院卫生、教育、劳工与养老金委员会副劳工政策主任、现任职于非营利组织Future of Life Institute的Wes McEnany称，周二的结果是对AI领域的“彻底否定”。他表示，AI触及人们生活的“方方面面”，无论是求职、使用社交媒体，还是住在数据中心附近时支付电费，人们厌倦了在相关对话中“没有任何 agency（话语权/能动性）”。

两党对数据中心建设的反弹是最具体的表现。周二选票上的44项地方数据中心禁令中，43项通过，向AI公司发出明确信号：在全国建设数据中心无疑将更加困难。在数据中心建设增长最快的关键战场州得克萨斯，候任州长Gina Hinojosa表示，她计划“发布暂停令——禁止——所有数据中心审批，直到立法机构通过保护得州人的法律”。其他几个关键州也作出类似承诺。Optro AI治理总经理Guru Sethupathy表示：“数据中心显然在选票上。”近几个月，越来越多抗议和两党集体行动反对在各州建设数据中心。居民担忧噪音污染、电费上涨等。NBC News周二对选民的民调显示，76%的人反对其社区建设数据中心。

推动AI监管的Super PAC“Guardrails Alliance”联合创始人兼主任Shaunna Thomas称：“数据中心反弹是我见过的最具两党共识的政治议题之一。”非营利科技行业监督机构The Tech Oversight Project副执行主任Kyle Jacobs-Morse表示，数据中心是审视更广泛企业问责的切入点：“我的账单涨了，为什么？”他说，人们发现大科技公司是罪魁祸首。他还称，尤其在得克萨斯、佐治亚和俄亥俄州长竞选中，民主党竞选团队优先关注数据中心带来的本地问题，包括对当地居民、社区和州政府的“溢出成本”。Golden Analytics创始人兼CEO François Ajenstat表示，他预计会听到更多关于“谁从AI受益、谁为AI买单”的问题，尤其是基础设施方面，但他更好奇监管会有什么变化。

专家称，中期选举结果可能终结特朗普和国会共和党人反复试图禁止州级AI限制的努力。Thomas认为这一想法“完全死了”；McEnany称，“任何投票抹除州AI法律的议员，下次选举都得找工作。”Jacobs-Morse预计总体上会看到更多“科技问责法案”。OpenAI最近开始将其数据中心称为“compute campuses（算力园区）”，特朗普总统9月曾试图将AI这一技术改名为“super intelligence（超级智能）”。但中期选举结果表明，相当一部分美国选民不买这些品牌重塑的账。Thomas说：“我不认为它奏效，而且选举后奏效的可能性极低。”Jacobs-Morse称，特朗普在这些事情上的“怪癖”“在票箱前表现不佳”。

不过，科技行业内外一些人对结果更为积极。一位X用户写道，“我们*也许*回到了作为一个理性、稳健国家的位置，可以真正发挥领导作用”；其他人称，近期结果可能有利于防止AI泡沫破裂。Glen Echo Group CEO兼Orchestra合伙人Katie Barr表示，她不会“过度解读”结果为对科技的压倒性拒绝，而应视为对“可负担性、就业、安全，以及人们能否对社区和生活中发生的事情有发言权”的清算。Yorkville Ives & Co.分析师在报告中写道，尽管科技投资者应准备迎接“AI和科技立法的重大障碍”，以及全国多达1000个数据中心的建设计划放缓，但也可能有“轻微正面”作用，即帮助避免泡沫并减缓资本募资涌入市场。

AI安全领域也可能出现清算。弗吉尼亚州民主党参议员Mark Warner以推动AI安全政策竞选并连任；佐治亚州民主党参议员Jon Ossoff在胜选演讲中称，“硅谷巨头为自己挖掘掩体，并警告他们正在创造的人工智能存在人类灭绝风险。”一些AI安全立法已在考虑中，例如9月佛蒙特州独立参议员Bernie Sanders和得克萨斯州民主党众议员Greg Casar提出的“禁止超级智能”法案。特朗普曾将AI安全危机斥为“骗局”，在社交媒体上写道，AI唯一需要的控制或“guardrails（护栏）”是“一个强大而聪明（高智商！）的总统”。但中期选举后，共和党议员将需要决定是跟随这一路线，还是与民主党就安全政策谈判。支持科技行业的倡导组织Chamber of Progress创始人兼CEO Adam Kovacevich表示，无论如何，他预计AI安全立法将继续在蓝州发生。他还说，民主党在科技政策上的下一步有很多开放问题：“我们是回到拜登时代对科技的战争、奥巴马时代的科技蜜月，还是介于两者之间？”

items.title: Into the Omniverse: How Developers Turn Ideas Into Simulations With Frontier AI Agents
items.description: Turning a simulation idea into a working application means assembling assets, connecting physics and rendering, and checking that the scene behaves as intended. Developers are combining frontier AI models with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to help carry out that work — building applications for exploring scenarios, investigating failures and improving designs. items.content: Turning a simulation idea into a working application means assembling assets, connecting physics and rendering, and checking that the scene behaves as intended. Developers are combining frontier AI models with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to help carry out that work — building applications for exploring scenarios, investigating failures and improving designs. Developers direct AI agents through natural-language instructions, review results and guide changes. Omniverse libraries provide GPU-accelerated physics, rendering and sensor simulation capabilities. Explore the projects below to see frontier AI models such as GPT-6 Astra at work, and check back for new examples from NVIDIA teams and developers across the ecosystem. Create Editable 3D Assets With Houdini and AI Agents 🔗 Creating animated 3D content requires connecting modeling, simulation, materials and rendering. Nick Scarcella, a senior technical artist on NVIDIA’s BondLab team, directed AI agents — primarily using Claude — to work with CUDA libraries and Isaac Sim to create animations. The BondLab team uses SideFX Houdini and the NVIDIA ovrtx library to develop materials, lighting and the final rendered appearance. In one experiment, Scarcella guided Astra to recreate an OP-1 portable synthesizer using product images, manuals and technical direction. He exported the model into the OpenUSD framework, tested it in Houdini and Blender, then used Astra and Opus to refine details before adjusting materials and textures for ovrtx rendering. Scarcella also used a publicly shared robot-hand checkpoint in Isaac Sim, directing the motion and developing materials and lighting in Houdini with Claude’s assistance. Working with team member Steven Dvornik, the team created an “Echos” visualization: translucent versions of the hand overlap and merge into a single hand animation, offering a visual interpretation of robot training. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Robot_Hand_Video_Omniverse.mp4 Figure: An artistic visualization of simulated robot-hand motion, developed with AI assistance and Houdini’s materials and lighting tools. These workflows bring agent-assisted creation into existing artist tools, giving teams editable content they can inspect, refine and render across applications. Explore Scarcella’s Houdini MCP tools and agent skill. Test Robotic Disassembly With Computer-Aided Design and Simulation 🔗 Before a robot can disassemble a product, developers need to know whether its tools can reach and remove the parts. Jens Jebens, a senior product manager for OpenUSD at NVIDIA, directed Astra to model a car suspension in PTC Onshape and configure it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim. Jebens used simulation feedback to revise the tooling, including a wrench designed to reach the suspension’s bolts, and reported successful removal of a suspension component in simulation. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Robotic_Dissasembly_Omniverse.mp4 PTC also connects computer-aided design (CAD) with simulation through Onshape’s SimReady Publisher, built with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Robotics startup Sensori uses it to transfer its Yuri robot into Isaac Sim, carrying geometry, joints and configuration data so the team can evaluate design changes without repeatedly rebuilding the simulation model. Read Sensori’s story. Explore the Onshape importer guide. Create an Editable Building Model From Site Scans 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/relay-video-v14-1080p.mp4 Planning warehouse automation requires a model of the building itself, but shelving and machinery can obscure its structure in site scans. Omniverse brings together real-to-sim tools and agent skills to help developers turn real-world captures into editable starting environments for physical AI simulation. David Wehr, from NVIDIA’s simulation technology team, built on that work using Astra to develop a workflow for digitally reconstructing a building without its contents. The goal is an editable, simulation-ready building model where developers can add or reposition shelving and machinery to evaluate warehouse layouts and automation plans before making physical changes. Wehr guided Astra to interpret panoramic photos, create building geometry and align it with point-cloud measurements. OpenUSD stores the models, while Omniverse’s ovrtx library renders results for inspection. Explore NVIDIA Omniverse agent skills to help agents build with Omniverse libraries. Test Gas-Turbine Operating Scenarios With a Digital Twin 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Turbine-Lab-RTX-and-What-If-under-10MB-1.mp4 Before changing how industrial equipment operates, engineers need a way to explore the consequences. Pradeep Kaushik, a member of the NVIDIA Omniverse developer relations team, directed Astra to build a what-if analysis application around a simulated gas turbine and generator. The application lets users adjust conditions such as load, ambient temperature and fuel composition, then compare power, efficiency, fuel consumption and equipment response. Six test procedures explore scenarios including load changes, a stuck fuel valve and an exhaust-sensor error. The prototype gives engineers an interactive way to investigate how operating changes and faults could affect equipment behavior, supporting decisions about which scenarios warrant further testing. Astra used tools like Cantera for thermochemistry and SciPy for equipment dynamics. The application maps solver results to rotor animation and color-coded temperature, pressure and flow-velocity indicators in a 3D turbine. NVIDIA Omniverse libraries update the scene (ovstage), render it with RTX (ovrtx) and stream the view to the browser (ovstream). Engineers can rotate and zoom the cutaway, switch between indicators, and pause or scrub through a simulated response alongside charts and virtual instruments. Build Simulation Scenes With Open Source SimReady Assets 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/kitchen_final_blog_with_music.mp4 With SimReady Central Library, announced at GTC Berlin, developers can access more than 2,000 simulation-ready USD assets from equipment manufacturers and asset providers for robotics simulations and AI factory digital twins workflows. Paul Kind, a member of NVIDIA’s Omniverse documentation team, pointed an AI agent to the library and guided scene assembly through conversation. His kitchen scene included 180 placements drawn from 63 unique library assets, alongside 18 custom geometry pieces. Kind reviewed renders produced with Isaac Sim and guided further adjustments. For robotics and factory workflows, developers can select SimReady assets with the simulation properties embedded to fit their required task then test in an assembled environment. Find assets in SimReady Central Library, and learn how to contribute. Stress-Test a Warehouse Simulation at Scale 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Infra-scale-demo-20260914_144614-Meeting-Recording.mp4 A warehouse simulation needs to keep running smoothly as more robot arms, conveyors and boxes fill the scene. When it slows down, developers need to identify what’s holding it back. Bhavik Sanganee, principal engineer at NVIDIA, used Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to build a warehouse simulation, increase its complexity and investigate slowdowns. Performance first fell below the target when the scene doubled in size. Running physics calculations, image rendering and video preparation concurrently restored performance and enabled further scaling. With 80 conveyors, 40 arms and 800 boxes, the simulation sustained 30 frames per second at full HD resolution during a two-minute test. The arms completed 640 successful box placements. Doubling the scene again reduced performance. Testing traced the slowdown to the physics and robot-control pipeline, giving Sanganee a specific area to improve. Start building with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Test Robot Control for Flexible Cable Routing 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/scurve_rl_vs_astra_side_by_side.mp4 In electronics assembly, a robot may need to position a flexible cable around components before plugging it into a port. The cable bends as the robot moves it, and the connector must line up precisely to fit. Oyindamola Omotuyi, robotics technical marketing manager at NVIDIA, directed Astra to build a robot simulation using NVIDIA Isaac Lab, Newton physics and Omniverse rendering with a Robotiq gripper handling the cable. Astra also developed a reinforcement learning system that combined learned cable-routing movements with position-and-orientation feedback and corrective adjustments for USB-C insertion. The simulation gave Omotuyi a way to test cable handling and connector alignment before moving to physical-robot experiments. The controller used information supplied directly by the simulation. Next steps include testing a friction-held grasp and using information a physical robot could obtain from cameras and sensors. Get started with robot learning in NVIDIA Isaac Lab. Turn Robot Computer-Aided Design Into a SimReady Asset 🔗 Before testing whether a robot can pick up and move a box, developers need a simulation model with joints that move correctly and with grippers that can hold the object. A computer-aided design (CAD) model provides the robot’s shape, but it still needs physics properties to perform the task. Using an ABB Robotics YuMi robot, developers directed Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse content libraries to convert CAD files into OpenUSD, match the robot’s appearance to reference images, and configure joints and collision geometry. They checked the asset against SimReady Foundation requirements before testing it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim. Both arms and grippers completed four cube pick-and-place cycles, using simulated finger contact and friction. These tests demonstrated behavior under the simulated conditions — estimated physical properties were not calibrated against the real robot. Follow the five-step SimReady tutorial. Build a Humanoid Simulator for a Warehouse Environment 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Humanoid-Warehouse.mp4 Explore a gamified, physics-based control of a humanoid robot in first- and third-person view. Before automating warehouse tasks, developers need an interactive simulation environment to explore task behavior and evaluate how the work gets done. Frank DeLise, Omniverse product manager at NVIDIA, used Astra to turn a SimReady warehouse and humanoid robot into an interactive simulator with first- and third-person views. DeLise directed Astra to connect NVIDIA Omniverse libraries for physics (ovphysx), scene updates (ovstage), rendering (ovrtx) and the user interface (ovui). He also used Astra with SimReady (simready-foundation) to create the physical scene in simulation. Astra then generated animation and application code to bring those capabilities together. Learn how to prepare and validate SimReady robot assets with frontier AI models and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Connect an Autonomous-Driving Testing Workflow 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/zero-to-alpamayo-under-10MB.mp4 Changing a scene, sensor or driving model can significantly affect autonomous-vehicle simulations. Doyub Kim, a manager on the simulation technology team at NVIDIA, asked Astra to build Zero to Alpamayo — a reusable simulation environment based on San Francisco’s Market Street. Kim directed Astra to map out the workflow, then connect asset creation, traffic, Omniverse RTX sensor simulation and Alpamayo driving in stages, checking each integration. The resulting prototype was a testing ground for comparing models and tracing how scene or sensor changes affect downstream driving behavior. A separate Cosmos3-Nano experiment varied weather and lighting in recorded simulation videos, allowing Kim to compare the driving model’s responses to the same scenario under different conditions. Use Sensor Differences to Create and Improve Digital Twins 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/0_00-0_004-hubble_rivermark_Real_Sim_no_loop.mp4 Comparing recorded and simulated camera and lidar outputs gives developers key performance indicator-based feedback for refining a scene. To test robots and autonomous vehicles, developers need to know how closely simulated sensors match real ones. Ashley Reid, who works on RTX sensor validation at NVIDIA, directed Astra and Claude Fable 5 agents to compare ovrtx camera and raw LiDAR outputs with recorded data. The agents created two digital twins from scratch and improved two existing ones. Over about three days, Reid guided an iterative workflow in which agents measured differences, created or modified OpenUSD scenes, and checked the results. Changes addressed missing objects, geometry and materials, with acceptance depending on camera and LiDAR metrics. This gives developers a way to use measured discrepancies to guide scene creation and improvement. Start by rendering an OpenUSD scene with the ovrtx minimal Python example, then define a sensor measure to compare with recorded data. Robo Olympics: Test Robot Skills With Simulation 🔗 Teaching robots new movements means checking whether those actions work under physical constraints. Tae Kim, who leads NVIDIA Omniverse engineering and product, used sports videos and natural-language instructions to guide Astra in building Robo Olympics, an experimental project that tests simulated Unitree G1 humanoids performing sports movements. Under Kim’s direction, Astra built controllers and refined them through physics trials. Newton Physics Engine simulated behavior, the open source NVIDIA Warp framework accelerated calculations and ovrtx rendered scenes and virtual-camera images. In one experiment, the robot cleared a single hurdle in 64 of 100 simulation trials. The trials gave Kim feedback for improving the robot’s timing and control. Watch Kim explore building simulations with Astra and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Bring the International Space Station Into the Browser 🔗 Turning 3D models into an application requires connecting assets, live data and an interface. Nic Johns, an engineering director at NVIDIA, prompted Astra to assemble NASA assets into an OpenUSD International Space Station model with telemetry. Johns built the application with a single prompt, then used a follow-up prompt to shift the scene to Earth’s daytime side so the planet was visible. The workflow used Blender for asset preparation and Omniverse libraries for rendering (ovrtx), scene runtime (ovstage) and streaming (ovstream). The application brings 3D models and operational data into the browser, with Johns guiding its development through prompts and corrections. Try the Omniverse Real-Time Viewer skill. Turn Captured Rooms Into Testing Environments 🔗 A digitally reconstructed room needs editable objects and accurate physical behavior before developers can test interactions. Chirag Majithia, from the Isaac engineering applications team at NVIDIA, directed Astra to turn stereo camera captures into an editable OpenUSD studio. The workflow combined PyCuSFM, FoundationStereo and nvblox for reconstruction, with user review guiding object selection and placement. Astra assembled generated and Blender-authored assets and used USD Content Agents to configure how objects move and interact in simulation. Isaac Sim tests guided collision and contact revisions for doors and drawers. The studio connects captured geometry to interaction testing, making gaps and object behavior easier to inspect. Explore USD Content Agents. Have a simulation idea? Explore NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to start building with an AI agent.
items.author: NVIDIA Writers
items.titleZh: 走进 Omniverse：开发者如何借助前沿 AI 智能体将想法转化为模拟
items.descriptionZh:
开发者正在将前沿AI模型与NVIDIA Omniverse库结合，通过自然语言指令驱动AI智能体完成仿真应用的搭建、审查和迭代。Omniverse库提供GPU加速的物理、渲染和传感器仿真能力，OpenUSD作为场景与资产的数据基础。文章展示了多个项目，说明这一范式如何覆盖从3D资产创建到机器人控制、工业数字孪生、自动驾驶测试和大规模场景性能优化。

在3D内容与资产创建方面，NVIDIA BondLab的Nick Scarcella主要使用Claude指挥AI智能体，结合CUDA库和Isaac Sim制作动画，并用SideFX Houdini与ovrtx库开发材质、灯光和最终渲染。实验中，Astra根据产品图片、手册和技术指导重建了OP-1便携合成器，导出到OpenUSD后在Houdini和Blender中测试，再用Astra和Opus细化细节并调整材质纹理以供ovrtx渲染。团队还利用公开的机械手检查点制作了“Echos”可视化，将半透明手部重叠融合为单一动画。类似地，开发者可将CAD模型转为SimReady资产：以ABB YuMi机器人为例，Astra将CAD转为OpenUSD、匹配外观、配置关节和碰撞几何，并按SimReady Foundation要求检查后在Isaac Sim中测试，双臂和夹爪完成四轮立方体抓放，依赖仿真接触和摩擦，但物理属性未与真实机器人校准。

机器人操作与装配方面，Jens Jebens让Astra在PTC Onshape中建模汽车悬架并在Isaac Sim中配置，利用仿真反馈修改工具，包括用于触及螺栓的扳手，最终在仿真中成功拆下悬架部件。PTC的Onshape SimReady Publisher基于Omniverse库连接CAD与仿真，机器人初创公司Sensori用其将Yuri机器人转入Isaac Sim，携带几何、关节和配置数据。Oyindamola Omotuyi则用Isaac Lab、Newton物理和Omniverse渲染构建线缆布线仿真，Astra开发了强化学习系统，将学习到的线缆布线动作与位置姿态反馈及USB-C插入修正结合，在进入物理机器人实验前测试线缆处理和连接器对齐。

工业与建筑数字孪生方面，Pradeep Kaushik指挥Astra围绕模拟燃气轮机和发电机构建what-if分析应用，用户可调整负载、环境温度和燃料成分，比较功率、效率、燃料消耗和设备响应；六种测试程序覆盖负载变化、燃料阀卡滞和排气传感器错误。Astra使用Cantera进行热化学计算、SciPy进行设备动力学计算，并将求解结果映射到3D涡轮的转子动画及颜色编码的温度、压力和流速指示。Omniverse库分别用ovstage更新场景、ovrtx以RTX渲染、ovstream将视图流式传输到浏览器。David Wehr则用Astra解读全景照片、创建建筑几何并与点云测量对齐，目标是生成可编辑、可用于仿真的建筑模型，以便在物理改造前评估仓库布局和自动化方案。Paul Kind利用GTC Berlin发布的SimReady Central Library，通过对话指导场景组装，厨房场景包含63个唯一库资产的180个放置和18个自定义几何体。

自动驾驶与传感器验证方面，Doyub Kim让Astra构建“Zero to Alpamayo”可复用仿真环境，基于旧金山Market Street，分阶段连接资产创建、交通、Omniverse RTX传感器仿真和Alpamayo驾驶模型，并逐项检查集成。另一项Cosmos3-Nano实验在录制的仿真视频中改变天气和光照，比较驾驶模型对同一场景不同条件的响应。Ashley Reid指挥Astra和Claude Fable 5智能体，将ovrtx相机和原始LiDAR输出与记录数据比较，约三天内迭代创建两个数字孪生并改进两个现有孪生，依据相机和LiDAR指标接受修改，用于指导场景创建和改进。

大规模场景性能方面，Bhavik Sanganee用Astra和Omniverse库构建仓库仿真并逐步增加复杂度。场景规模翻倍时性能首次低于目标；同时运行物理计算、图像渲染和视频准备后恢复性能并继续扩展。在80条传送带、40个机械臂和800个箱子的配置下，仿真在1080p全高清下持续两分钟保持30帧/秒，机械臂完成640次成功箱子放置。再次翻倍后性能下降，测试将瓶颈定位到物理和机器人控制管线。Tae Kim的“Robo Olympics”项目用体育视频和自然语言指导Astra构建Unitree G1人形机器人运动测试，Newton物理引擎模拟行为，开源Warp框架加速计算，ovrtx渲染场景和虚拟相机图像；一次实验中机器人100次试验成功跨过单栏64次。

此外，Nic Johns用单条提示让Astra将NASA资产组装为带遥测的OpenUSD国际空间站模型，并用后续提示将场景切换到地球白天侧，工作流使用Blender准备资产，ovrtx渲染、ovstage场景运行时和ovstream流式传输。Chirag Majithia则用Astra将立体相机捕获转为可编辑OpenUSD工作室，结合PyCuSFM、FoundationStereo和nvblox重建，USD Content Agents配置物体运动和交互，Isaac Sim测试指导门和抽屉的碰撞与接触修正。Frank DeLise用Astra将SimReady仓库和人形机器人变成支持第一/第三人称视角的交互式模拟器，连接ovphysx、ovstage、ovrtx和ovui。

总体来看，这些项目表明AI智能体与Omniverse库的组合正在降低仿真应用开发门槛：开发者用自然语言描述意图，智能体负责连接资产、物理、渲染、传感器和界面，并可通过仿真指标迭代。应用场景覆盖机器人训练与验证、自动驾驶测试、工业设备分析、仓库自动化规划、电子装配、建筑重建和太空资产可视化。SimReady Central Library的2000多个仿真就绪USD资产进一步支持机器人仿真和AI工厂数字孪生工作流。当前部分结果仍依赖仿真条件，物理属性尚未与真实设备校准，后续需要将仿真中获得的控制器和模型迁移到带摄像头和传感器的物理机器人。

items.content: The AI-generated sci-fi film Gods Don’t Give Gifts has added a bit of star power: Pop star Grimes is going to appear in the movie. Billed as “the first AI film to come to theatres,” Gods Don’t Give Gifts is a notable test case for the commercial potential of AI films, and it releases on December 4th. Grimes — who will be lending both her likeness and vocal performance to the movie, which you can see in the clip above — potentially gives the project some legitimacy.AI studio Fable, which is producing the film, claimed in a press release that “casting the likeness of an actor with their spoken vocal performance will become more common with animated films using AI: audiences will see actors, athletes, musicians giving vocal performances with their likeness in films.” Gods Don’t Give Gifts is being directed by Jack London, better known under the online handle Gossip Goblin.RelatedThe 2.5-hour AI-generated Odyssey movie is 2.5 hours too longGods Don’t Give Gifts is an anthology that’s set in a future “where bodies are disposable and consciousness has been commoditized” and depicts what happens when “four interconnected stories collide with the horrifying consequences of humanity’s attempt to transcend the flesh.” Those themes seem to fit pretty snugly with Grimes’ interests, as she has explored themes of transhumanism and artificial intelligence in the past. It’s also not the only AI project she’s working on, with an AI-themed album called Psy Opera in the works.Here’s the trailer for Gods Don’t Give Gifts:While there has been plenty of hype around the potential for AI in Hollywood, there’s yet to be a project that shows that the technology is actually a vital storytelling tool. Previous examples, like two different takes on The Odyssey — including one made with Elon Musk’s Grok — have left plenty to be desired.
items.author: Andrew Webster
items.titleZh: 格莱姆斯将主演一部即将登陆影院的人工智能电影
items.descriptionZh:
AI生成科幻电影《Gods Don’t Give Gifts》宣布流行歌手Grimes将参演，为这部自称“首部登陆院线的AI电影”增添了明星关注度。影片将于12月4日上映，被视为检验AI电影商业潜力的重要案例。Grimes不仅将授权其形象（likeness），还将为影片提供声音表演；原文视频片段展示了相关效果。制作方AI工作室Fable在新闻稿中称，未来“让演员以其形象和声音表演出现在AI动画电影中”会越来越常见，观众将看到演员、运动员、音乐人以自身形象配合声音表演出现在电影里。影片由Jack London执导，他在网上的昵称是Gossip Goblin。

从技术路径看，该项目并非传统真人拍摄或纯手工动画，而是利用生成式AI制作动画电影，并把明星的授权形象与语音表演结合到AI生成角色中。其创新点主要在于“明星形象+声音表演”的AI选角模式，以及尝试让AI生成电影进入院线发行渠道。原文未披露制作成本、所用模型、渲染分辨率、帧率等具体性能参数，因此难以进行量化技术对比；但可以确定的是，影片的核心卖点是AI生成内容与明星IP的结合，意在借助Grimes的公众形象和声音表演提升项目合法性与市场吸引力。

《Gods Don’t Give Gifts》是一部 anthology 式作品，故事设定在一个“身体可被抛弃、意识已被商品化”的未来，讲述四个相互关联的故事如何与“人类试图超越肉体”的可怕后果发生碰撞。这些主题与Grimes过去对超人类主义和人工智能的兴趣较为契合；她还在制作一张AI主题专辑《Psy Opera》。这表明该项目不仅是技术演示，也试图用科幻叙事包装AI与意识、身体商品化等议题。

商业与行业影响方面，该片是对AI电影能否吸引院线观众的一次测试。此前好莱坞对AI充满炒作，但尚未有项目证明该技术是“至关重要的叙事工具”。已有案例包括两个不同版本的《奥德赛》改编，其中一个使用马斯克的Grok制作，但效果“仍有很大不足”；另一部2.5小时AI生成《奥德赛》也被评论为“2.5小时太长”。这些对比说明，AI电影目前仍面临时长控制、叙事质量和观众接受度等挑战。若《Gods Don’t Give Gifts》能借助Grimes的明星效应获得关注，可能推动更多AI动画电影采用“演员形象+声音授权”的模式，并引发关于表演授权、版权、劳动替代和院线发行标准的进一步讨论。

items.title: Chinese AI lab Moonshot reportedly looked at European data centers to access Nvidia chips, report claims
items.description: The lab is reportedly interested in renting at least 8,000 Nvidia Blackwell GPUs.
items.content: Share Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Moonshot AI, the Chinese lab that made Kimi, is reportedly looking towards Europe to gain access to the latest Nvidia Blackwell AI GPUs. According to CNBC, the company is in talks with at least one European data center to lease clusters with 8,000 or more GPUs for inferencing, and that it’s also interested in securing compute capacity for training.Go deeper with TH Premium: AI and data centers (Image credit: Microsoft)The data center cooling state of playThe custom AI ASIC state of play America’s AI chip rules keep changing — and the rest of the world is paying the priceGTC 2026: Ian Buck press Q&A transcript — VP of Hyperscale and HPC speaks out on shelving CPX and shipping LPU decode this yearDemand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsibleWhile Chinese companies are banned from acquiring Nvidia Blackwell and other AI GPUs that offer the same or better performance containing U.S. technologies, a loophole has so far allowed them to gain access to compute by renting them from data centers abroad. The U.S. House is attempting to patch it and passed the Remote Access Security Act, but it must still go through the Senate and the White House before it can turn into law. In the meantime, Chinese AI labs are exploiting the loophole and training their models on foreign data centers that have acquired Nvidia chips.The U.S. and China have been locked in an AI arms race, with the latter’s open-weight models behind frontier U.S. models by just a matter of months. More importantly, these models, like Kimi K3, are significantly easier to run and could even be much cheaper to use. These advancements happened despite Washington’s efforts to make it harder for Chinese AI labs to acquire hardware that uses American technologies through export bans. But even though President Donald Trump eventually made a 180-degree turn and allowed Nvidia H200 chips for export to China, Beijing has taken steps to protect its domestic AI chip industry by blocking H200 imports at the border, meaning these companies must look elsewhere if they want to access the latest, most powerful AI GPUs to train their models.Latest Videos FromTom's HardwareWatch full video here: Moonshot also has a limited window if it wants to secure compute capacity outside of China — Nvidia has reportedly told its data center clients to limit their business and avoid serving more than 49% of their capacity to Chinese outfits. This could be a harbinger of things to come, especially as reports like these could spotlight the bipartisan bill and increase pressure to advance the legislation sooner rather than later. items.titleZh: 报道称中国AI实验室月之暗面曾考察欧洲数据中心以获取英伟达芯片
items.descriptionZh:
据CNBC报道，开发Kimi系列模型的中国AI实验室Moonshot AI正与至少一家欧洲数据中心洽谈，计划租用拥有8000块或更多GPU的集群用于推理，并对获取训练算力表现出兴趣。这一动向的核心背景是：美国禁止中国公司直接购买英伟达Blackwell等包含美国技术、性能相当或更强的AI GPU，但中国公司仍可通过租用海外数据中心的算力获得类似能力，形成事实上的远程访问漏洞。美国众议院已通过《远程访问安全法案》试图堵住该漏洞，但法案仍需参议院和白宫批准才能成为法律；在此之前，中国AI实验室正利用海外数据中心已采购的英伟达芯片训练模型。

从技术路线看，报道并未披露Moonshot AI在Kimi K3上的具体架构或训练方法，重点在于其算力获取策略：通过欧洲数据中心租用大规模Blackwell集群，分别服务模型推理和训练。Kimi系列属于开放权重模型，报道称其与美国前沿模型的差距仅数月，且Kimi K3更易于运行、使用成本可能显著更低，这构成中国开放权重模型的重要竞争力。性能参数方面，原文只给出8000块以上GPU的集群规模、英伟达据称要求数据中心客户对华业务不超过其容量的49%，以及中国开放权重模型落后美国前沿模型“几个月”等对比信息，未提供具体基准测试、租赁价格或训练规模数据。

应用场景上，8000块以上GPU的集群可支撑大规模推理服务，降低Kimi模型对外服务的延迟和成本，也可用于后续模型训练，维持迭代速度。技术影响在于：若远程租用算力模式持续，中国AI实验室可在不直接购买受控芯片的情况下获得先进算力；但美国立法和英伟达对数据中心客户的对华业务限制可能压缩这一窗口。与此同时，中美AI竞赛仍在延续。报道称，美国政府后来转向允许英伟达H200对华出口，但北京为保护国内AI芯片产业在边境阻止H200进口，使中国企业更倾向寻求海外最新GPU算力。整体来看，Moonshot AI的欧洲寻租计划是出口管制、远程算力漏洞、美国立法进程与中美AI竞争共同作用下的典型案例，也可能增加美国推动《远程访问安全法案》落地的政治压力。

items.title: The Wizard of Open Weights: Chris Alexiuk Makes AI Easy With Open Models
items.description: Chris Alexiuk has a simple rule about open source AI: If you believe in it, be loud about it. “We should be shouting about this technology from the rooftops,” said Alexiuk, a Toronto-based senior product research engineer in deep learning at NVIDIA who specializes in making open large language models (LLMs) practical for working developers.  […]
items.content: Chris Alexiuk has a simple rule about open source AI: If you believe in it, be loud about it. “We should be shouting about this technology from the rooftops,” said Alexiuk, a Toronto-based senior product research engineer in deep learning at NVIDIA who specializes in making open large language models (LLMs) practical for working developers. Alexiuk’s preferred “rooftop” is YouTube, where he’s built a following teaching curious thousands how to build, fine-tune, evaluate and ship production LLM applications and agents. “I think the people who will most help us understand how to build and apply AI likely haven’t even heard of it yet,” he said. “Trying to get knowledge and information out to as many people as humanly possible is what continues to drive me.” Bringing NVIDIA Nemotron to Developers Everywhere Having spent years teaching developers to build with open models, Alexiuk has concluded that transparency isn’t a feature of good AI; it’s the precondition for it. “Fully open source AI is necessary for the democratization of intelligence,” he said. “You should have access to the weights, the data that went into it, the training recipes, everything.” That’s why, on his LinkedIn profile, Alexiuk styles himself “No. 1 Nemotron Fan,” referring to the NVIDIA Nemotron family of open source, multimodal models built for long-running, self-evolving and specialized AI agents. “I think Nemotron is the most important project that exists,” said Alexiuk, who also uses the pseudonym “Joe Nemotron” across social media. “I’m a firm believer that openness is a very important thing to undertake, so I’m going to be the No. 1 fan of whoever is doing that the best. And that is Nemotron.” https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/ChrisAlexiuk_captions_9MB.mp4 It’s this matter-of-fact directness and affable approachability that makes Alexiuk’s teaching style so appealing. On the social media platform X, he goes by the handle “llm_wizard.” His avatar: a laughing cartoon caricature sporting a slouchy sorcerer’s hat and brandishing a magic wand. It’s no surprise, then, that Alexiuk likens Nemotron to a magical library — its users fellow wizards in search of knowledge that can move mountains. “You’re a wizard in search of prepared spells, and Nemotron has a spell for everything,” he said. “Just choose the one you need.” In non-wizard terms? “There’s a category of model that’s going to be close to the kind of work you want to accomplish,” Alexiuk said, explaining that Nemotron supports that whole ecosystem of AI users: from individual developers using a model like Nemotron 3.5 Lightning for repetitive, high-frequency execution work to a company deploying Nemotron Ultra for long-running autonomous agents, deep research and enterprise tasks. NVIDIAN Chris Alexiuk (left) engages with developers during the Build-a-Claw event at GTC Berlin. “I think that openness helps more people understand AI and hopefully leads to more people doing really ingenious things with these tools at the limit,” Alexiuk said. “If a tool is amplifying skill, it’s amplifying human expression.” From Birding to Model-Building Alexiuk first became fascinated with machine learning in a computational physics class at Trent University in Ontario, Canada. “After that, I learned about TensorFlow and that you could build image classifiers that ran on your GPU,” he recalled. As an initial one-off project, Alexiuk built a classifier that would alert him whenever his friend’s distinctive pet bird, a Yellow-Faced Gray Budgerigar, appeared in frame on his webcam during shared video game sessions. “Because we were playing video games, I wasn’t focused on my friend’s webcam, but I didn’t want to miss seeing the bird when it appeared,” Alexiuk said. “And then my whole life changed, because in that instance I realized it’s crazy what you could do with technology.” Since then, he’s been embedding himself in the open source AI community. “To imagine within the span of a few years going from freaking out because I could know my friend’s bird was in the camera frame to being able to make any website in a matter of minutes with a model that’s running on my laptop — I cannot wait to see what’s next,” Alexiuk said. “It’s never been more accessible to get into and learn about AI.” And if another LLM wizard arises to challenge him for the title of No. 1 Nemotron Fan? “It would be the greatest day of my life to be surpassed by an even bigger fan of Nemotron, who had heard about Nemotron through the work I was doing,” Alexiuk said. “That would be a capstone to my career that I can only dream of.” Hear more from Alexiuk by following the NVIDIA Nemotron Labs Livestreams series on YouTube.
items.author: Matthew Leib
items.titleZh: 开放权重奇才：克里斯·阿列克修克用开放模型让 AI 变得简单
items.descriptionZh:
NVIDIA深度学习高级产品研究工程师Chris Alexiuk是开源AI的积极倡导者。他认为，真正开放的人工智能不能只开放部分接口，而应让开发者获得模型权重、训练数据、训练配方等完整信息，这是“智能民主化”的前提。Alexiuk目前在NVIDIA专注于让开放大语言模型更适用于一线开发者，并通过YouTube、LinkedIn和X等平台教授开发者如何构建、微调、评估和部署生产级LLM应用与智能体。他在社交媒体上自称“No.1 Nemotron Fan”，还使用“Joe Nemotron”这一化名，X账号名为“llm_wizard”，以轻松直白的方式向更广泛人群传播开源模型知识。

新闻的核心是NVIDIA Nemotron模型家族。根据报道，Nemotron是NVIDIA推出的开源多模态模型系列，面向长时间运行、自我演化和专业化的AI智能体。Alexiuk将其比作“魔法图书馆”：开发者可以按任务需求选择合适模型。具体而言，Nemotron 3.5 Lightning适合重复性、高频率的执行类工作；Nemotron Ultra则面向长时间运行的自主智能体、深度研究和企业级任务。这一分层定位覆盖了从个人开发者到企业部署的多种AI工作负载。其创新点主要不在单一模型架构，而在于以完全开放的方式提供权重、数据和训练配方，使开发者能够审查、复现、微调和二次开发模型，并把开源透明作为构建可信AI的基础条件。原文没有展开Nemotron的具体网络架构、参数量或训练方法细节。

在性能参数和对比数据方面，这篇报道未披露Nemotron各模型的具体基准成绩、参数量、推理吞吐、成本或与其他模型的量化对比，因此无法从原文判断其性能优劣。新闻主要传递的是产品定位和生态理念：通过不同规格的Nemotron模型覆盖高频轻量任务与长时复杂任务，让开发者根据实际需求选择，而不是依赖单一通用模型。Alexiuk强调，开放模型能帮助更多人理解AI，并推动开发者在工具能力边界上做出更有创造性的应用。

从技术影响和应用场景看，Nemotron可用于生产级LLM应用和智能体开发、模型微调与评估、企业自主代理、深度研究以及高频自动化执行等。Alexiuk的个人经历也体现了AI工具门槛的下降：他在加拿大特伦特大学的计算物理课上接触机器学习，后来用TensorFlow和GPU构建图像分类器，用来识别朋友在视频通话中出现的黄脸灰虎皮鹦鹉。从那时起，他深入参与开源AI社区。他认为，如今从学习AI到用笔记本上的模型快速构建网站和应用，技术可及性已显著提高；开源工具若能放大开发者技能，也就是在放大人类表达。对于“No.1 Nemotron Fan”可能被超越，他表示欢迎，认为如果有更多人通过他的工作了解并成为更狂热的Nemotron支持者，将是其职业生涯的理想注脚。整体来看，这是一篇以人物故事切入的NVIDIA开源AI生态传播报道，重点在开源理念、开发者教育和Nemotron模型家族的应用定位，而非技术基准发布。

items.title: More Performance From Every Byte: How Full-Stack Codesign Solves AI’s Memory Challenge
items.description: Larger models, longer contexts and agentic applications are increasing GPU memory pressure while supply tightens and prices rise — a trend expected to continue through the near term. NVIDIA works closely with memory partners to rapidly adopt the latest memory technologies. NVIDIA was first to adopt HBM3e and HBM4 technologies into an accelerated computing stack.  […]
items.content: Larger models, longer contexts and agentic applications are increasing GPU memory pressure while supply tightens and prices rise — a trend expected to continue through the near term. NVIDIA works closely with memory partners to rapidly adopt the latest memory technologies. NVIDIA was first to adopt HBM3e and HBM4 technologies into an accelerated computing stack. But the approach isn’t to simply pack more memory onto the GPU. It’s full-stack codesign. NVIDIA intentionally designs GPUs, CPUs, networking, storage and software together to get more useful work out of memory at every layer of the AI factory. That matters because an AI factory runs on a memory and storage hierarchy. GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM) is the fastest, most expensive and most contested tier — with model weights and KV cache competing for limited capacity. Below it sit CPU memory, local SSDs and shared storage, each trading speed for more capacity at a lower cost per bit. How much useful work a byte does depends on how well the whole hierarchy is used: shrinking what must be stored, placing it on the right tier and bringing it back to the GPU before it’s needed. Byte for byte, NVIDIA makes the most efficient use of memory at every layer — and the results show it. From NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra to the Vera Rubin platform, HBM capacity per GPU rose roughly 3%, while agentic throughput per dollar rose by up to 30x on SemiAnalysis AgentX. Agentic Inference Is Putting More Pressure on HBM Frontier models now have trillions of parameters — the values that hold what an AI model learned in training. KV cache, which holds the context the model needs to understand each active request without reprocessing the same information, is also expanding. Agentic trajectories carry prior context across repeated model and tool calls, in some cases processing up to 3 million tokens, so each request’s working memory grows over time. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) adds relevant enterprise information to prompts, creating even more context to process and retain. During inference, HBM primarily holds both model parameters and KV cache. The result: greater pressure on HBM. Why AI Factories Need a Memory Hierarchy Adding more HBM capacity per GPU is the obvious response to that pressure, but capacity delivers only what bandwidth can move. Think of HBM as a warehouse and memory bandwidth as its loading docks. A larger warehouse holds more inventory, but the docks set how much can move in and out at a time. Once the docks are at capacity, moving more inventory takes longer and slows response times. If delays exceed the required service level, the added space can’t be used effectively, even as it adds cost and draws power. That’s also why no operation keeps all its inventory in the closest, fastest space. What’s in motion stays near the line. What’s waiting moves to a larger, cheaper space nearby and returns before it’s needed. An AI factory faces the same limit. More HBM can hold more KV cache and support more concurrent users. Every added user shares the same compute and memory bandwidth. But when each user expects fast responses, eventually memory bandwidth is unable to supply data as fast as compute can use it: a limit engineers call the memory wall. Past that point, extra HBM capacity can’t be put to work, yet it still adds costs and draws power. The data still needs a place to live, but not all of it needs the fastest, most expensive tier. This is why an AI factory manages data across a memory and storage hierarchy. Maximizing the Value of Every Byte With Full-Stack Codesign NVIDIA’s full-stack codesign makes every byte of HBM count by relieving pressure from model weights, KV cache and RAG data. It does this with techniques that each target a different source of inefficiency: Shrink model weights and distribute them across the NVL72 domain. The NVFP4 format reduces the space required for weights compared to FP8, the lowest precision possible on the NVIDIA Hopper platform. Recent models, including FLUX.2 [klein] from Black Forest Labs, Inkling from Thinking Machines Lab, Beam 1.0 from Reflection, Meta Muse Spark from Meta, Step 5 Preview from StepFun and NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL have been released with NVFP4 checkpoints, demonstrating growing model-builder adoption of 4-bit precision for faster, more memory-efficient inference. Within an NVL72 system, model weights can be distributed across up to 72 GPUs, so each GPU holds a smaller share of the model — leaving more HBM for KV cache and concurrent users. Shrink KV-cache and offload inactive context to lower-cost storage tiers. Applying NVFP4 to the KV cache reduces its footprint compared with FP8, so more context can stay resident in HBM. NVIDIA Vera CPU helps in two ways. Faster tool execution shortens the time KV cache sits inactive during tool calls, and its large LPDDR memory, connected to NVIDIA Rubin GPUs over NVIDIA NVLink-C2C interconnect, gives paused context a nearby place to wait and return quickly. When context isn’t actively in use, NVIDIA Dynamo inference software moves it to NVIDIA CMX context memory storage — a tier built for capacity at far lower cost per bit than HBM — and returns it before reuse. Unlike local SSDs, CMX is shared across servers, and unlike enterprise storage, it skips the overhead of long-term data protection that short-lived context doesn’t need. NVIDIA CMX context memory storage partners include Cloudian, DDN, Dell Technologies, Everpure (previously Pure Storage), HPE, IBM, NetApp, VAST and WEKA. Dynamo’s KV Cache Reuse ties the tiers together, managing KV cache as one system-wide resource across GPU memory, CPU memory and storage, so context computed once can be reused across the system. Compact RAG embeddings and keeping the index outside HBM. RAG turns enterprise documents into embeddings — numerical representations that let a system search by meaning rather than keyword — organized into a searchable index. NVIDIA Nemotron Retriever models produce smaller embeddings with higher retrieval accuracy, while the NVIDIA cuVS library enables that index to be built and served across CPU and storage. The knowledge base never occupies HBM, and only the passages the model needs enter context. The result is less HBM used for model weights, less HBM tied up by idle context and more of it available to serve concurrent users. More Useful Output per Dollar With Each Generation Across successive NVIDIA platform generations, tokens per second per dollar has risen far faster than HBM capacity. On the SemiAnalysis AgentX DeepSeek V4 Pro workload, NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 delivers up to 10x higher throughput per dollar than NVIDIA H200 platform at 100 tokens per second per user, with HBM capacity per GPU roughly doubling. At 125 tokens per second per user, Vera Rubin NVL72 delivers up to 30x higher throughput per dollar than GB300 NVL72, with HBM capacity per GPU up about 3%. For AI factory operators, the metric that matters is how many useful tokens the factory can deliver within its power budget while meeting user response-time needs. More tokens per second per watt means more work and revenue from the same power, and a lower cost for every token. NVIDIA’s full-stack codesign lowers token costs by increasing the useful work every byte of memory delivers. Learn more in the video explainer and technical deep dive on how NVIDIA full-stack codesign reduces inference memory pressure.
items.author: Amr Elmeleegy
items.titleZh: 从每个字节中释放更多性能：全栈协同设计如何解决AI的内存挑战
items.descriptionZh:
随着大模型参数规模进入万亿级、上下文窗口不断拉长，以及智能体（agentic）应用兴起，GPU内存压力持续上升；与此同时，内存供给趋紧、价格上涨，这一趋势预计短期内仍将延续。英伟达正与内存合作伙伴紧密协作，快速采用最新内存技术，并率先将HBM3e和HBM4引入加速计算栈。但其思路并非简单地在GPU上堆叠更多内存，而是进行全栈协同设计：将GPU、CPU、网络、存储和软件一起设计，使AI工厂每一层内存都能完成更多有用工作。

AI工厂运行在内存与存储层级之上。GPU高带宽内存（HBM）是最快、最贵、竞争最激烈的层级，模型权重和KV缓存争抢有限容量；其下依次是CPU内存、本地SSD和共享存储，以速度换容量、降低每比特成本。一个字节能完成多少有用工作，取决于整个层级是否被高效利用：缩小必须存储的内容、将其放在正确层级，并在需要之前送回GPU。英伟达称，从Blackwell Ultra到Vera Rubin平台，每GPU的HBM容量仅增长约3%，但在SemiAnalysis AgentX上，每美元智能体吞吐量最高提升30倍。

智能体推理正在给HBM带来更大压力。前沿模型已有数万亿参数，KV缓存也在扩张，它保存模型理解每个活跃请求所需的上下文，避免重复处理相同信息。智能体轨迹会在反复的模型和工具调用中携带先前上下文，某些情况下处理多达300万token，因此每个请求的工作内存会随时间增长。检索增强生成（RAG）还会把相关企业信息加入提示，产生更多需要处理和保留的上下文。推理期间，HBM主要承载模型参数和KV缓存，结果是对HBM的压力进一步加大。

增加每GPU的HBM容量是直观应对方式，但容量只提供带宽所能搬运的数据量。可以把HBM比作仓库，把内存带宽比作装卸码头：仓库更大能存更多库存，但码头决定单位时间进出多少；码头满负荷后，搬运更多库存会更慢并拖慢响应时间。如果延迟超过所需服务水平，新增空间就无法有效利用，反而增加成本和功耗。AI工厂同样如此：更多HBM可容纳更多KV缓存、支持更多并发用户，但每个用户共享相同的计算和内存带宽；当用户期待快速响应时，内存带宽最终无法以计算所需速度供给数据，即“内存墙”。超过这一点，额外HBM容量无法投入工作，却仍增加成本和功耗。数据仍需存放，但并非所有数据都需要最快、最贵的层级，因此AI工厂必须在内存和存储层级间管理数据。

英伟达通过全栈协同设计，从模型权重、KV缓存和RAG数据三方面缓解HBM压力，让每个字节更有价值。第一，缩小模型权重并跨NVL72域分布。NVFP4格式相比FP8减少权重所需空间，FP8是英伟达Hopper平台可实现的最低精度。Black Forest Labs的FLUX.2 [klein]、Thinking Machines Lab的Inkling、Reflection的Beam 1.0、Meta的Muse Spark、StepFun的Step 5 Preview以及NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL等近期模型已发布NVFP4检查点，显示模型厂商越来越多采用4位精度以实现更快、更省内存的推理。在NVL72系统中，模型权重可分布到最多72块GPU上，每块GPU只保留较小份额，从而为KV缓存和并发用户留出更多HBM。

第二，缩小KV缓存，并把不活跃上下文卸载到低成本存储层级。对KV缓存应用NVFP4可较FP8降低占用，使更多上下文常驻HBM。Vera CPU从两方面提供帮助：更快的工具执行缩短KV缓存在工具调用期间处于不活跃状态的时间；其大容量LPDDR内存通过NVLink-C2C互连连接Rubin GPU，为暂停的上下文提供就近等待并快速返回的位置。当上下文不活跃时，Dynamo推理软件将其移至NVIDIA CMX上下文内存存储——这一层级为容量而建，每比特成本远低于HBM——并在再次使用前返回。与本地SSD不同，CMX可跨服务器共享；与企业存储不同，它跳过短期上下文不需要的长期数据保护开销。CMX合作伙伴包括Cloudian、DDN、Dell Technologies、Everpure（原Pure Storage）、HPE、IBM、NetApp、VAST和WEKA。Dynamo的KV Cache Reuse将各层级连接起来，把KV缓存作为跨GPU内存、CPU内存和存储的系统级资源统一管理，使一次计算出的上下文可在整个系统中复用。

第三，压缩RAG嵌入并把索引放在HBM之外。RAG把企业文档转化为嵌入，即让系统按语义而非关键词搜索的数值表示，并组织成可搜索索引。NVIDIA Nemotron Retriever模型能生成更小的嵌入并提高检索精度，NVIDIA cuVS库则支持在CPU和存储上构建并服务该索引。知识库因此不占用HBM，只有模型需要的段落进入上下文。最终，更少HBM用于模型权重，更少被闲置上下文占用，更多HBM可用于服务并发用户。

从性能对比看，跨代平台的每美元每秒token数增长远快于HBM容量增长。在SemiAnalysis AgentX的DeepSeek V4 Pro工作负载上，当每用户100 token/s时，GB300 NVL72的每美元吞吐量最高可达H200平台的10倍，而每GPU HBM容量约翻倍。当每用户125 token/s时，Vera Rubin NVL72的每美元吞吐量最高可达GB300 NVL72的30倍，而每GPU HBM容量仅增长约3%。对AI工厂运营者而言，关键指标是在功率预算内、满足用户响应时间要求的前提下能交付多少有用token；每瓦每秒更多token意味着同样功率下更多工作和收入，以及更低的每token成本。英伟达的全栈协同设计通过提升每字节内存所完成的有用工作，降低token成本，并缓解智能体推理、长上下文、RAG和企业知识库等场景下的内存压力。

items.title: The hidden supply chain costs of the AI boom
items.description:
Today, I’m talking with Willy Shih, an economist, a professor of management practice at Harvard Business School, and the author of the upcoming book, Where Does My Stuff Come From? The Powerful Economics Behind Global Supply Chains.
Willy is one of my all-time favorite Decoder guests — his way of looking at the world through our supply chains is just a fascinating way of making sense of the global economy. I first met Willy in 2019, while The Verge was covering Foxconn’s promise to build an LCD fab in Wisconsin. That obviously never happened, but Willy called it right away because he could see the supply chain to support a fab simply wasn’t in place. We also had Willy on the show in 2021 to talk about what was then the pandemic-era chip shortage.
Now, five years later, we’re in another manufacturing mess, as we stand in the middle of a political fight over whether globalization is coming to an end. Trumps’ tariffs keep changing, the factories that were supposed to reshore in America mostly haven’t materialized, and AI is devouring the planet’s computing resources during an unprecedented infrastructure buildout.
Willy’s new book is all about the economics underlying these complex systems, which our politicians and regulators seem to insistently ignore. You’ll hear us talk about why the markets have reacted to all these disruptions the way they have, and why China remains a global manufacturing powerhouse even though every other country thinks that’s so risky. I loved this conversation — it’s in the weeds, and Willy really knows his stuff.
Okay: economist Will Shih on his new book Where Does My Stuff Come From? Here we go.


This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. 
Willy Shih, you’re an economist and professor of management practice at Harvard. You’re also the author of the new book, Where Does My Stuff Come From: The Powerful Economics Behind Global Supply Chains. Welcome back to Decoder.
Well, thanks for having me back.
I am very excited to talk to you. You and I first started talking ages ago when The Verge was covering Foxconn in Wisconsin. You are a reliable source of information on what it takes to actually build an LCD plant anywhere, not just in Wisconsin.
The Foxconn in Wisconsin thing was funny because I tend to go on first principles on these things. Once I knew they weren’t going to build a glass plant across the street, it’s like there’s no way there’s going to be a factory.
Now, what happened afterwards, of course, is people heard your show, and then I started getting calls from people who live in the community. They went to the zoning hearings in town, then sent me the plans and asked, “Is this going to be a panel factory?” I said, “No, I told you it’s not going to be a panel factory.” So they sent me the plans. I said, “Well, there’s not enough concrete to make this a panel factory.” For a panel factory, you need stability, so you gotta have all this structural steel, and you have to have all this concrete.



Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here. 
My favorite part of the Foxconn story — and I don’t mean to rehash it, but it’s just fun to talk to you about it again — is when you said there’s not enough concrete and steel. It’s great. We should actually talk about LCD manufacturing a little bit. There’s an entire chapter in your book about why all of it is in China and China’s investment in that. But I want to just take a big step back for a second.
It seems to me that you’ve written a book about the end of globalization in one particular way. We had big global supply chains. The pandemic came and shocked the just-in-time manufacturing system to its core. And then the Trump administration, in the second round, has imposed a whole bunch of tariffs.
I’ve had several guests on the show straightforwardly tell me we’re de-globalizing the economy. That’s what’s happening here. We can’t rely on it anymore. Your book, as you read it, is a little bit of a reaction to that, but you’re also pointing out how globalization is one of the smartest ways to do it based on first principles of economics.
Tell me about the state of the world and the state of our supply chains right now from your point of view.
Well, I think the point about first principles of economics is actually spot on. I often tell people my father was an economist, and I used to see him come home from work, and I thought, “I never want to do that. I’m going to go into science and technology.” So I went into science and technology and took all these engineering classes. And I was in product businesses only to discover, to my horror, that if you don’t get the economics right, then it doesn’t matter for science and technology.
The book’s subtitle is “the powerful economics behind global supply chains.” I talk about all these principles behind global supply chains, but they’re all actually driven by economics. In fact, what you see today is market forces responding to all this stuff.
So, for example, when we put tariffs on stuff coming out of China, then manufacturers say, “Okay, let me move that supply chain, and I’ll do my assembly in Vietnam, or I’m going to do my assembly in Mexico, or let me find some way to circumvent these tariffs.” What I really find is that when you look at how these supply chains are structured, like why do cashew nuts say they come from Vietnam when they were actually grown in the Ivory Coast or Ghana? Well, there was an economic reason for all of these things. It’s why frozen fish that are caught off the coast of Alaska go to Qingdao, China, for processing before they come back. Again, it’s because it’s cheaper to do it that way.
When we put up these trade barriers, the first reaction tends to be, “How can I circumvent that?” We saw a lot of that, especially last year. I remember Liberation Day was April 2nd, and if you look at the quarter right before, people knew stuff was going to be happening.
We have this circumvention going. That’s why in the first quarter of 2025, we had all-time-record imports from Ireland, and then the first half of 2026 showed slow imports from Ireland. That’s because we’re burning off all the stuff we imported in the first half of 2025.
It all gets down to economics. I’m getting all these TV set ads because the holiday season is coming up. Great, and they’re all coming from Mexico. It’s like, “How can they all be coming from Mexico?” I know the flat panel factories that supply all these TV sets these days are all in China, and they’re all in China because the plants have been subsidized so heavily or because of industrial policies that have encouraged those plants to be there.
If you watch the trade lanes, you’ll see this stuff. What happens is there’ve been all these new shipping routes from China to Mexico over the last two years. Direct ocean container service from China to Mexico. It’s like, “Huh, I wonder what that’s about.” I’ll tell you what it’s about. It’s about moving parts and components from China to Mexico so that I can assemble them in Mexico and then bring them in under the USMCA agreement.
So what you’re actually seeing is that these supply chains are organized the way they are partly because some places have the capabilities, but more often than not, a lot of these are just responding to economic forces. If I’m going to add on tariffs or I’m going to make it more expensive to ship something between two points, the market will find a way around that.
That’s something I want to come back to several times in this conversation. “It’s cheaper” was a real driving force of globalization. Americans like cheap things. They like cheap flat-panel TVs. The fact that I can go to Costco right now and get a 50-inch TV for $300 is a miracle of the modern supply chain and of modern manufacturing.
It is a miracle, right? And it’s cheaper, and it’s because there’s a place that, for better or for worse, can make it cheaper. By the way, American consumers benefit from that.
One of the reasons that we pursued free trade and globalization so heavily in the United States is that we thought that creating economic ties between all these various countries would reduce the potential for an armed conflict. There are a lot of ways to think about that, but in general, if you tie the economies together, the price of having a war shoots up, and then you won’t have free or cheap TVs, and maybe the public won’t like that.
That is under pressure now, right? We’re sitting here in the middle of an AI conversation, where China is routinely invoked as the great threat that will rise up if they get to AGI before us. We are putting up tariffs, particularly on China. In the United States, the policy administration is to bring manufacturing back to the United States through the use of tariffs. Your point of view is that simple economics will provide enough contortions to avoid that blunt outcome.
When we seal the borders for some products everywhere, then the price is going to go up. So, for example, putting tariffs on steel. Initially, when we just put tariffs on imported steel and aluminum, then what happened was, “Well, gee, I happen to be making construction equipment. More than half of the cost of that construction equipment is medium carbon steel, so therefore it makes it easier for me to import construction equipment from somewhere else.” We then say, “Okay. Now we’re going to tariff stuff based on your steel content.”
Eventually, when you close off all those things, which means you’re basically tariffing everything, then stuff gets more expensive domestically. You could look back on the period from 2000 until really 2012 to 2014; we had relatively low inflation. Part of it is because we were getting cheaper stuff from China.
I think there are a couple of things that drove a breakdown of this model, if you will. One is that people didn’t really recognize that the connection between moving work out of the US to China meant you’re leaving people behind who don’t have any more work. That cost was spread over people who, by the way, also shop at Walmart and benefit from the cheap goods. But we as a country didn’t think about it like, how are we going to retrain all those people who weren’t making furniture in North Carolina or who were making castings and forgings in Kentucky or wherever?
That was one part of the problem. The other part of the problem is that we have this gigantic trade deficit. Now, a lot of that is fueled by government spending and borrowing and so on. But typically, in some respects, you would’ve expected the exchange rate or some other adjustment mechanism to compensate for that.
I remember the last time exchange rates moved was in the 1980s. That was also the last time the US ever had a trade surplus, when the dollar got a lot cheaper relative to the Japanese yen, especially at that time. That had an adjustment on trade flows as well.
So now you have China running this ginormous trade surplus. Basically, what they’re doing is exporting their economic problems in China to the US, and they’re exporting that at the expense of jobs elsewhere. The Europeans have suddenly woken up to that. Now go to a place like Germany, where half the economy revolves around the auto industry, and they now have figured it out, and it’s like, “Wait a minute, this is an existential crisis for us.”
But on those two things, the controls you would’ve expected to rebalance things didn’t pan out. That’s why we have so much discussion about this right now and a view of this as a problem.
It feels like my entire teen experience was a conversation about NAFTA, and we should open free trade in North America. Later on, I got to college, and all the economic discussion was about the EU and creating the single market in the EU: “We’re going to set up these big open markets, and there’s going to be free trade inside of those markets, and that will lead to a kind of economic prosperity.”
Fast forward to 2026, and the desire to tear a lot of that down has gone way up, right? Particularly as you look at the USMCA and Chinese goods coming to Mexico to come to the United States, nakedly circumventing the entire policy goal of imposing tariffs. 

The goal is to build the iPhone in the United States. The goal is to build manufacturing in the United States. I know that you have never really thought that’s an achievable goal, but that is the goal. That is what the administration promised. We’ve created these trade groups, trade associations, that allow that goal to be circumvented. Do you think the walls are going to keep going up, or do you think they’re going to come back down?
I think we’re going to see more pressure to moderate our behavior a little bit because, let’s face it, there are a lot of goods that we, as a country, need access to inexpensive labor. So I’m actually very pro-USMCA as a successor to NAFTA because I actually think there are things that we need inexpensive labor for. Mexico is a good place to source things like that. There are things that we need from Canada.
So if we were to look at North America as a trading bloc, then what you would see is the benefits of specialization, which is the whole rationale for trade in the first place. We’re better at doing this, you’re better at doing that; you specialize in that, we’ll specialize in this. We trade; everybody is better off. If you can do that with a community of countries that understand the need for that type of balance, then everybody is better off.
I think the problem with China is they’re very happy to have this imbalance, where they want the world to be dependent on them, but they don’t want to buy stuff from the rest of the world. When you have that, then trade doesn’t really work. So I think that’s the problem.
I’m hoping we’re going to realize that we’re better off among a group of like-minded countries where we can trade within that bloc. So for example, if the US were to view North American partners and European partners in Japan — and countries in Southeast Asia, Australia, New Zealand, parts of Central and South America, and even Africa — and say, “Okay, let’s trade across this bloc,” then we’d have access to most of what we need, whether it’s critical minerals, low-cost labor, or a lot of technology specialties. We could do much better with that, much better than a go-it-alone strategy in my view.
The first part of your book — which I highly recommend the audience read; it’s a fun read — is just setting up the first principles of why we trade at all in the very concept of labor arbitrage. It seems like we’re having a national policy conversation that is 500 steps removed from these basic ideas of why we would trade.
It is entirely centered around: can you bring manufacturing back to America because we let all the manufacturing jobs go to Mexico and China, particularly in high tech? And we’re behind. There might be some extraordinarily bad event, like a war, where it’s exposed how little manufacturing capability we have in the United States.
That has nothing to do with the basics of specialization in various countries around the world. It’s another problem, and the blunt instrument is, “Boy, it’s bad that all of our drones are made in China. We’re going to prevent drones from being sold here.
