Of course, our industry will set up drone manufacturing in the United States.” I don’t see that connection. Do you see that working?
No. I think that’s a transactional view where you look at one piece at a time as opposed to looking at the bigger picture. I think we have to start with a core principle that the US is a high-cost country. Therefore, if you want manufacturing jobs coming to the US, then you’ve got to have high labor productivity.
In fact, if you look at the types of jobs that are coming back to the US, they tend to use a lot of automation, a lot of sophisticated manufacturing processes, and stuff that is high-skill that can justify the high labor cost. Either that, or they are things where we have a technological lead that nobody else knows how to do in the world.
I was looking at the high-temperature superalloys that are used in the hot section of jet engines. There are only three companies in the world that know how to cast those, and two of them are in the US, and one of them is in the UK. There are things like that the rest of the world has to buy from us. So if you have high labor productivity or highly differentiated products, those we can make in the US; we can make them successfully. By the way, most of them never left the country.
The US, France, and the UK are major suppliers of jet engines to the entire world market. Even the Chinese buy those from the West. So if we have these things that we do better than anybody else, we should invest in those and make sure that we’re always in the lead, and then everybody else will buy from us, and then you’ll have some balance where you can’t be held up.
There’s a lot of this thinking like, “I wish I could turn the clock back to the 1980s or the 1970s, when manufacturing was the path to the middle class in the US.” But manufacturing has changed worldwide, and for those jobs that you want to have manufacturing in the US, you’ve got to have high labor productivity or the high differentiation that’ll go with it.
I want to stay on the iPhone for one more second. Apple just inked a new deal where they’re going to source a bunch of titanium from a Pennsylvania-based company called Perryman for the iPhone 18 Pro and the new iPhone Duo. They’re going to source that titanium here. They’re then going to ship it to China. They’re going to assemble the phone in China, and they’re going to ship the phones back to us. They do that with Corning and glass as well.
I’ve always looked at that. Tim Cook’s job, in particular, is that he’s a statesman. He has to negotiate with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping about iPhone production and tariffs in these supply chains, and the iPhone holds the global economy together. If the price of the iPhone gets too high because of tariffs, maybe there’s an electoral impact in the United States.
How do you see products like that? Are they as load-bearing as it feels to me, or are they just examples of the larger system?
I think the iPhone is a terrific example of how difficult this problem is. Because right now you have components that have high technological complexity. The iPhone uses the most advanced chips produced by Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company. By the way, most of those chips are still going to be made in Taiwan. TSMC has a fab in Arizona, but its capacity is piddly compared to what it has in Taiwan.
Those chips come from one place and require the most sophisticated processing tools that come from ASML in the Netherlands, but also companies like Lam Research and Applied Materials in the US. So it’s that global thing. But the key thing is iPhones also require assembly labor. They require manual assembly because we’re not at the point yet where you can assemble the whole thing with a robot.
There’s actually a chapter in my book where I talk about what Henry Ford and the lifestyles of the Chinese Communist Party have to do with assembling iPhones. It turns out it’s a lot. The lifestyles of the Chinese Communist Party have to do with how they mobilize workers in what’s called the Danwei model, which was established after the Communist Revolution. It’s where you have a production site, a walled city with housing for workers, a means of production, warehouses, ways to feed them, and stuff like that.
If you ever go to a phone factory in China, the real question is: how do I mobilize 100,000 to 200,000 workers to do this manual assembly on a scale that an Apple needs? They’re trying to do it in India. They’re having some success with India, but that was really hard. Once again, it’s: how do I mobilize manual labor at that level of scale?
So the iPhone, as you point out, is a great example of a global product because it needs the highest level of tech, and it also needs the huge workforce to do the manual assembly.
There’s actually a great book called Apple in China, which I also recommend. The narrative is that the Chinese government subsidized an awful lot of manufacturing in China. They built these cities, and they built the culture that enables the labor at scale. Your example in the book, again, is LCD factories, where the Chinese government invested in overcapacity, and that drove the price of LCD manufacturing down. Basically, it’s all centered in China now.
The flip side of that is, boy, it’s pretty obvious that they stole a bunch of American intellectual property along the way. They developed these manufacturing capabilities. They took a lot of the know-how that Apple imported into that country. They did the same with Tesla in a lot of ways. They stood up an entire electric car industry on the back of the innovation Tesla had started through manufacturing in that country. Now they have those capabilities, and they’re racing ahead of our companies because we don’t actually have the manufacturing know-how.
Can you rebalance that? I hear this concern a lot: that you can’t rebalance it. If all the manufacturing happens there, they will actually be state-of-the-art, and we will fall behind.
I’m not sure if “stole” is the best description of how they got these capabilities. I would say they learned it, and in many cases we taught it to them. Being a supplier to Apple is often referred to as a golden ticket, and people say, “Well, why is it a golden ticket?” Well, obviously you get cash flow from selling products to them.
But the other thing is that Apple is a real taskmaster. By making you work hard to improve your products, improve your specs, meet their performance specs, and meet their cost targets, you get better. The same thing happened when Tesla set up their factory in Shanghai. The fact that they qualified local suppliers raised the game in the Chinese EV market.
Another thing I think a lot of people miss about China is that there is actually this very interesting competition going on. Beijing sets policies and objectives, but then all the regional governments, the provinces, and the major cities are competing with each other. They set up this free market dynamic, and so you have this fierce competition between regions.
The regions are also very smart about setting objectives. They keep raising the bar for people so the technology gets better. You have a dynamic where there’s really cutthroat competition in the Chinese market, and it’s about survival to make better products at lower prices. That’s something that’s really driving it right now.
To your point about how, to the extent we’ve lost the ability to make things, the Chinese have a lot of capabilities. You should walk through some Chinese factories these days. They’re way ahead of the US in terms of using automation, because they’re investing like crazy.
I had a student I was talking to about his father’s factory in Shanghai, and he said his father’s answer to everything, every competitive threat, was just more CapEx: “I’m going to throw more capital at it. I’m going to buy the latest machine.” I was in one factory a couple of months ago where the equipment was two or maybe three years old, and they were ripping it out and upgrading it to the latest generation because they said, “This is how we’re going to survive. We have to make the product more efficiently, and we have to make a better product.”
So there’s this internal competition in the Chinese marketplace that is really fearsome, and it’s hard for Western companies to compete there, but that is an important dynamic that’s going on as well.
The interesting thing about that, as I compare and contrast China with the United States, is that the system in China is understood. It’s stable. You can make a lot of criticisms of that system. I think you can make an endless number of human rights criticisms of the Chinese government. It’s obviously a repressive government in a lot of ways.
But the economic system is understood, and it’s controlled at the top in a meaningfully stable way. The goals are apparent, the investment is apparent, and there’s a lot of competition to achieve those goals with that investment.
There are two things about that which I think are significant. The first is that China engages in long-term planning, five-year plans. Now, when I was a kid, I used to look at China’s five-year plans, and I thought, “This is a big joke,” because they would make a lot of mistakes, like Mao Zedong’s Great Leap Forward, and they were doing this new type of tillage in farming, and they caused this huge famine and millions of people died.
But to the credit of the government there, when they do this type of long-range planning, they learn from their mistakes, and they get better. If you look at their current five-year plans and the last couple of five-year plans, they’re good plans. They understand what’s important, and they focus on those things that are important.
Then the second point is about what kinds of people they have implementing these plans. I was in one of these third-tier cities some number of years ago, and I was having dinner with the economic development commission there. At the beginning of dinner, I said, “Hey guys, just for fun, let’s go around the table and talk about what you studied in school.” It was mechanical engineering, industrial engineering, electrical engineering, metallurgy, metallurgy, mechanical engineering. You go to Washington and ask what people studied in school, and it’s political science, economics, and government.
So you have these technocrats competing in technology-intensive businesses and having that understanding. By the way, that’s one of the reasons I wrote this book: I was serving on these committees appointed by the Commerce Secretary on supply chains, and I realized we have civil servants who don’t have the exposure to supply chains and how stuff is actually made.
China had this plan that was called the 863 plan. The 863 plan was when four scholars went to the government in Beijing in March of 1986 — that’s why it’s called “863”; it was ‘86, March. I remember the first time I looked at the 863 plan, and it was, “If we want to be a modern economy, we have to be good at these things.”
I looked at that plan in the 1990s, and I said, “This is a good plan.” And they’ve executed every one of those things. They said, “We need to be good at all these things, like information technology, biotechnology.” In semiconductors, they still have a way to go, but they identified civil aircraft. But they identified all these different technologies like communications technology, software, and robotics.
I would contrast that with the Trump administration here in Trump’s second term, where… We already talked about Liberation Day. Howard Lutnick is on television saying, “We’re going to move manufacturing back to the United States. This is the goal of the tariffs.”
Three weeks later, there are 900 lawsuits about the tariffs, and Howard Lutnick is back on TV saying, “Robots will do all the manufacturing now. This is the goal. We’re going to do heavy automation.” And then the tariffs get struck down, and they find a new law for different tariffs.
It does not seem like the same long-term planning that can be stuck to, or the same environment where businesses understand the stability of the trading system such that they can compete ferociously. Every CEO who does manufacturing and comes on the show usually ends up talking to me about how they scrambled to buy RAM at affordable prices to make their products, which has to keep them from doing anything else.
How would you contrast that? Can we get out of this moment where it’s a pure scramble, or is this fully shaking everything up?
We’re in a very transactional environment. Everything is short-term, and these rapid changes that you see in the tariffs… If you look at a map of 2025 and 2026 and put a dot everywhere there was some tariff action, it looks like a shotgun hit the wall. There are all these spots all over the place.
The problem with that is when you have that type of instability, it’s very hard for a company to make any long-term plans. Before I build a factory, I want to know that I’m going to have stable demand for a couple of years, at least until I have a chance of earning a return on that thing. I’ve talked to a couple of companies about this. These were overseas companies thinking about coming into the US market, and they said, “Well, I can’t do it because things keep changing. Do I go to Mexico? Do I go to the US? What part of the US do I go into?”
Especially with things like semiconductor fabs, you need to know that you’re going to be able to get 10 to 20 years out of it. When things change every couple of weeks, what that does instead is say, “I’m just going to hold off on an investment because it’s just too uncertain. It changes too often.”
Are you seeing that slow down in investment? Are you seeing companies say, “We can’t actually invest in manufacturing in the United States”?
It varies. I see that with a lot of companies asking, “Where do I want to put my production operations?” Okay, now we see some things like car plants coming into the US, and usually that’s a function of the pain being too great.
But the whole auto tariff thing is also a little bit crazy. If you look historically at production strategies in the auto industry, typically when you build a plant, you size it to build about 200,000 to 250,000 units of a model or a model family, because that’s like the efficient scale for an auto plant.
Then what you have is a company like BMW that says, “Great, I’m going to build all my X Series SUVs in South Carolina. I’ll build the 3 Series somewhere else. I’ll build the 5 Series somewhere else, and I’ll build the 7 Series somewhere else. And then what I’ll do is exchange them.”
So BMW in South Carolina or Mercedes in Alabama, they build certain models in the US, export them to the rest of the world, and then import other models so that you have the whole product line. Toyota does that. For example, they build more Camrys in the US than anywhere else, and they were exporting some of those as well.
But then when you start putting tariffs on imports, that screws up that whole strategy. Again, it’s a decision that was made without understanding how the automakers had laid out that strategy.. You need to understand how the supply chain is structured and why it’s structured the way it is, and then you can be more thoughtful..
Do you see tariffs as mostly protectionist? I was in France earlier this year, and I took an Uber, and I think it was a BYD Seal, a Chinese EV. I asked the French Uber driver, “How do you like this car?” He was very French, and he literally did the thing. He goes, “Peugeot is shit.” I almost started clapping because it was amazing. He’s like, “If the French government would just allow the Chinese government to sell these cars here, these companies would all be dead.”
In the United States, I think Jim Farley, the CEO of Ford, is running around saying the Chinese EVs are superior to American products. It’s the tariffs that protect our markets and protect our manufacturers, because you could import the cars, but you’d pay such high tariffs that they’re economically infeasible.
That’s just pure protectionism. That goes against what you’re saying, which is that you need to protect your industry until their products are good enough to compete on the global scale. But we’re not doing that with our carmakers. We’re just protecting them.
Yeah, and there’s a cost associated with that. So, for example, one of the famous tariffs is a so-called chicken tax. I talk about this in the book as well. The chicken tax resulted from this trade spat where we put tariffs on imported light trucks.
SUVs are built on that platform. It’s one of the reasons the Detroit automakers have focused on SUVs and light trucks. That’s their profit center because there’ve been tariffs on that, and it’s only happened in the last decade or so that Toyota and Nissan and others have made more light trucks in the US and Mexico. So that’s one of the results of that type of tariff distortion.
Wait. But that’s a policy victory, right? Toyota, Nissan, and all the other foreign manufacturers are going to make trucks in the United States. You’ve gotten some economic benefit; they can compete, and maybe all the trucks are going to get better.
You get some economic benefit, but one of the reasons the Detroit guys still make so many trucks and SUVs on those platforms is because they’re more profitable, which says the price is higher than it might otherwise have been. But I do see the benefit of that.
Although I have to say, I was walking around the Toyota factory in Georgetown, Kentucky. I’m walking around with the plant manager, and I said, “You’re making sedans here?” He said, “Yep,” and a lot of the Detroit guys have given up making sedans because they can’t make any money. I said, “And you’re using parts that mostly come from Kentucky, Ohio, Indiana, Alabama, Mississippi, and Texas, and some from Mexico and Japan, but mostly domestic content.” He’s like, “Yep.” I said, “And you’re using American workers.” He said, “Yep.” I said, “You’re using American-made steel.”
I’m trying to get out of him that, okay, look, I know American steel costs a lot more than imported steel because I’ve been in other factories that are still importing steel despite the steel tariffs because they say it’s still cheaper in Asia. But I said, “You’re using American-made steel.” So I’m trying to get that out of him: how much he’s paying for steel.
Obviously, he’s not going to tell me, but he does say, “We have a strategic long-term relationship with our supplier.” That tells you a lot, which is that there are ways you can do these things. You have to work with your suppliers. You have to give them longer-term arrangements, be less transactional, more strategic on things like that. So I think you can do it, but it really takes a comprehensive and more thoughtful approach.
I understand the rationale for putting tariffs on foreign goods that undercut our markets. You’re just going to increase the cost, and then maybe the consumer will buy the domestic product, and that’s better for our economy. It just hasn’t seemed to have worked.
I don’t see Liberation Day as having done anything except generally raise prices on everything. We haven’t actually remapped the global economy. And a lot of what you’re describing is, well, the system is pretty resilient. The system was pretty resilient to COVID. The system was pretty resilient to an oil tanker getting stuck in the Suez Canal. The system has been pretty resilient to the war in Iran. The system has been pretty resilient to absolutely chaotic tariffs.
Maybe some prices have risen, and I’m sure we’re going to get listeners pointing out that all the prices have risen. It feels like the only thing the system isn’t resilient to is the AI industry wanting every scrap of RAM that the whole world can produce. And so now there’s not going to be inexpensive cell phones.
What will push the system over the breaking point? Because globalization has seemed generally resilient to a bunch of people who want it to be over.
I think what you’re highlighting is that it’s really the power of the market. In the case of closing the Strait of Hormuz, Brent North Sea crude prices didn’t go to $150 a barrel like I was afraid they would, and a lot of people were afraid they would because the market adjusted.
We applied a lot of tariffs on Liberation Day. The first response was circumvention or front-running. The next response was tariff engineering. The next response is like, “Okay, let me move production to Vietnam or let me move production to Mexico, and I’ll find a way around that.” Now, eventually, when you close down all those things, then prices eventually have to rise.
In the case of memory chips, that’s a different problem because the demand far outstripped the capacity. I used to always buy memory cards on Black Friday. Forget that this year.
Yeah, it’s all over.
I’m just glad I stocked up on a previous Black Friday.
If you want to know my prediction for when the AI industry will meet its true political end, it’s when Grand Theft Auto VI comes out. Everyone goes out to buy a PS5, and they realize it’s more expensive now at the end of its life cycle than it was at the beginning because the price of memory has skyrocketed.
Yeah, no kidding. We’re talking about huge amounts. But that’s the same thing. We’re in a phase where we see all these tactical actions taken by the government, very transactional, without necessarily understanding all the complex interconnections and interdependencies.
You may have noticed, for example, that the administration temporarily suspended the Jones Act. I don’t know if you remember that. Why did they temporarily suspend the Jones Act? Because oil refineries on the East Coast of the US couldn’t get their oil from Texas cheaply because there were no domestic supertankers.
The Jones Act requires that if you move stuff from Texas to New Jersey, you have to have a US-owned, US-crewed, US-built, very large crude carrier. There aren’t any because we don’t build those in the US. So that’s why it’s cheaper to bring oil from Algeria to New Jersey than it is to bring it from Texas. And that’s why they suspended the Jones Act for a while. At least they understood that.
I know at least some of our audience is going to be listening to this conversation, and you’re steeped in global trade. You wrote a book to educate our government about how it works from the basics, which I think is sorely needed.
But a lot of the promise for young people in our politics lately is that we will rebuild American capacity. We will rebuild manufacturing capacity. We will bring back a bunch of jobs where you don’t need an advanced degree in AI prompt engineering or whatever to see the future. We will bring back the dignity of work.
Politicians on both sides are making these promises all the time, and a lot of that requires closing down trade, forcing that economic activity back within our borders. It just seems like that isn’t likely. So I’m not going to ask you whether or not that is totally likely. I’m going to ask: what’s more likely instead?
Well, I think what’s more likely is that we will see efforts as you describe. I would love to sit down with people and say, okay, we want to move this type of production back to the US. Let’s take a more strategic, more nuanced approach, understanding the bigger picture, considering what levers are available.
The US is still a big, attractive market. It is the largest market in the world. It is the most attractive market in the world. That’s, by the way, why the Chinese all want to come here: because they can make some money here that they can’t make elsewhere. So then how do we harness that market power and that market pull with a more nuanced understanding of why our supply chains are organized the way they are today? Recognizing that, can I build a strategy to bring important things that are very strategic for the US to know how to do?
Let’s think about how we fix this problem with an understanding of that bigger picture.
Willy, it’s been great to talk to you. It is always just a pleasure. We have to have you back faster than five years. Thank you so much for being on Decoder.
Thanks for having me.
Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email!
items.content: Today, I’m talking with Willy Shih, an economist, a professor of management practice at Harvard Business School, and the author of the upcoming book, Where Does My Stuff Come From? The Powerful Economics Behind Global Supply Chains.Willy is one of my all-time favorite Decoder guests — his way of looking at the world through our supply chains is just a fascinating way of making sense of the global economy. I first met Willy in 2019, while The Verge was covering Foxconn’s promise to build an LCD fab in Wisconsin. That obviously never happened, but Willy called it right away because he could see the supply chain to support a fab simply wasn’t in place. We also had Willy on the show in 2021 to talk about what was then the pandemic-era chip shortage.Now, five years later, we’re in another manufacturing mess, as we stand in the middle of a political fight over whether globalization is coming to an end. Trumps’ tariffs keep changing, the factories that were supposed to reshore in America mostly haven’t materialized, and AI is devouring the planet’s computing resources during an unprecedented infrastructure buildout.Willy’s new book is all about the economics underlying these complex systems, which our politicians and regulators seem to insistently ignore. You’ll hear us talk about why the markets have reacted to all these disruptions the way they have, and why China remains a global manufacturing powerhouse even though every other country thinks that’s so risky. I loved this conversation — it’s in the weeds, and Willy really knows his stuff.Okay: economist Will Shih on his new book Where Does My Stuff Come From? Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Willy Shih, you’re an economist and professor of management practice at Harvard. You’re also the author of the new book, Where Does My Stuff Come From: The Powerful Economics Behind Global Supply Chains. Welcome back to Decoder.Well, thanks for having me back.I am very excited to talk to you. You and I first started talking ages ago when The Verge was covering Foxconn in Wisconsin. You are a reliable source of information on what it takes to actually build an LCD plant anywhere, not just in Wisconsin.The Foxconn in Wisconsin thing was funny because I tend to go on first principles on these things. Once I knew they weren’t going to build a glass plant across the street, it’s like there’s no way there’s going to be a factory.Now, what happened afterwards, of course, is people heard your show, and then I started getting calls from people who live in the community. They went to the zoning hearings in town, then sent me the plans and asked, “Is this going to be a panel factory?” I said, “No, I told you it’s not going to be a panel factory.” So they sent me the plans. I said, “Well, there’s not enough concrete to make this a panel factory.” For a panel factory, you need stability, so you gotta have all this structural steel, and you have to have all this concrete.Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.My favorite part of the Foxconn story — and I don’t mean to rehash it, but it’s just fun to talk to you about it again — is when you said there’s not enough concrete and steel. It’s great. We should actually talk about LCD manufacturing a little bit. There’s an entire chapter in your book about why all of it is in China and China’s investment in that. But I want to just take a big step back for a second.It seems to me that you’ve written a book about the end of globalization in one particular way. We had big global supply chains. The pandemic came and shocked the just-in-time manufacturing system to its core. And then the Trump administration, in the second round, has imposed a whole bunch of tariffs.I’ve had several guests on the show straightforwardly tell me we’re de-globalizing the economy. That’s what’s happening here. We can’t rely on it anymore. Your book, as you read it, is a little bit of a reaction to that, but you’re also pointing out how globalization is one of the smartest ways to do it based on first principles of economics.Tell me about the state of the world and the state of our supply chains right now from your point of view.Well, I think the point about first principles of economics is actually spot on. I often tell people my father was an economist, and I used to see him come home from work, and I thought, “I never want to do that. I’m going to go into science and technology.” So I went into science and technology and took all these engineering classes. And I was in product businesses only to discover, to my horror, that if you don’t get the economics right, then it doesn’t matter for science and technology.The book’s subtitle is “the powerful economics behind global supply chains.” I talk about all these principles behind global supply chains, but they’re all actually driven by economics. In fact, what you see today is market forces responding to all this stuff.So, for example, when we put tariffs on stuff coming out of China, then manufacturers say, “Okay, let me move that supply chain, and I’ll do my assembly in Vietnam, or I’m going to do my assembly in Mexico, or let me find some way to circumvent these tariffs.” What I really find is that when you look at how these supply chains are structured, like why do cashew nuts say they come from Vietnam when they were actually grown in the Ivory Coast or Ghana? Well, there was an economic reason for all of these things. It’s why frozen fish that are caught off the coast of Alaska go to Qingdao, China, for processing before they come back. Again, it’s because it’s cheaper to do it that way.When we put up these trade barriers, the first reaction tends to be, “How can I circumvent that?” We saw a lot of that, especially last year. I remember Liberation Day was April 2nd, and if you look at the quarter right before, people knew stuff was going to be happening.We have this circumvention going. That’s why in the first quarter of 2025, we had all-time-record imports from Ireland, and then the first half of 2026 showed slow imports from Ireland. That’s because we’re burning off all the stuff we imported in the first half of 2025.It all gets down to economics. I’m getting all these TV set ads because the holiday season is coming up. Great, and they’re all coming from Mexico. It’s like, “How can they all be coming from Mexico?” I know the flat panel factories that supply all these TV sets these days are all in China, and they’re all in China because the plants have been subsidized so heavily or because of industrial policies that have encouraged those plants to be there.If you watch the trade lanes, you’ll see this stuff. What happens is there’ve been all these new shipping routes from China to Mexico over the last two years. Direct ocean container service from China to Mexico. It’s like, “Huh, I wonder what that’s about.” I’ll tell you what it’s about. It’s about moving parts and components from China to Mexico so that I can assemble them in Mexico and then bring them in under the USMCA agreement.So what you’re actually seeing is that these supply chains are organized the way they are partly because some places have the capabilities, but more often than not, a lot of these are just responding to economic forces. If I’m going to add on tariffs or I’m going to make it more expensive to ship something between two points, the market will find a way around that.That’s something I want to come back to several times in this conversation. “It’s cheaper” was a real driving force of globalization. Americans like cheap things. They like cheap flat-panel TVs. The fact that I can go to Costco right now and get a 50-inch TV for $300 is a miracle of the modern supply chain and of modern manufacturing.It is a miracle, right? And it’s cheaper, and it’s because there’s a place that, for better or for worse, can make it cheaper. By the way, American consumers benefit from that.One of the reasons that we pursued free trade and globalization so heavily in the United States is that we thought that creating economic ties between all these various countries would reduce the potential for an armed conflict. There are a lot of ways to think about that, but in general, if you tie the economies together, the price of having a war shoots up, and then you won’t have free or cheap TVs, and maybe the public won’t like that.That is under pressure now, right? We’re sitting here in the middle of an AI conversation, where China is routinely invoked as the great threat that will rise up if they get to AGI before us. We are putting up tariffs, particularly on China. In the United States, the policy administration is to bring manufacturing back to the United States through the use of tariffs. Your point of view is that simple economics will provide enough contortions to avoid that blunt outcome.When we seal the borders for some products everywhere, then the price is going to go up. So, for example, putting tariffs on steel. Initially, when we just put tariffs on imported steel and aluminum, then what happened was, “Well, gee, I happen to be making construction equipment. More than half of the cost of that construction equipment is medium carbon steel, so therefore it makes it easier for me to import construction equipment from somewhere else.” We then say, “Okay. Now we’re going to tariff stuff based on your steel content.”Eventually, when you close off all those things, which means you’re basically tariffing everything, then stuff gets more expensive domestically. You could look back on the period from 2000 until really 2012 to 2014; we had relatively low inflation. Part of it is because we were getting cheaper stuff from China.I think there are a couple of things that drove a breakdown of this model, if you will. One is that people didn’t really recognize that the connection between moving work out of the US to China meant you’re leaving people behind who don’t have any more work. That cost was spread over people who, by the way, also shop at Walmart and benefit from the cheap goods. But we as a country didn’t think about it like, how are we going to retrain all those people who weren’t making furniture in North Carolina or who were making castings and forgings in Kentucky or wherever?That was one part of the problem. The other part of the problem is that we have this gigantic trade deficit. Now, a lot of that is fueled by government spending and borrowing and so on. But typically, in some respects, you would’ve expected the exchange rate or some other adjustment mechanism to compensate for that.I remember the last time exchange rates moved was in the 1980s. That was also the last time the US ever had a trade surplus, when the dollar got a lot cheaper relative to the Japanese yen, especially at that time. That had an adjustment on trade flows as well.So now you have China running this ginormous trade surplus. Basically, what they’re doing is exporting their economic problems in China to the US, and they’re exporting that at the expense of jobs elsewhere. The Europeans have suddenly woken up to that. Now go to a place like Germany, where half the economy revolves around the auto industry, and they now have figured it out, and it’s like, “Wait a minute, this is an existential crisis for us.”But on those two things, the controls you would’ve expected to rebalance things didn’t pan out. That’s why we have so much discussion about this right now and a view of this as a problem.It feels like my entire teen experience was a conversation about NAFTA, and we should open free trade in North America. Later on, I got to college, and all the economic discussion was about the EU and creating the single market in the EU: “We’re going to set up these big open markets, and there’s going to be free trade inside of those markets, and that will lead to a kind of economic prosperity.”Fast forward to 2026, and the desire to tear a lot of that down has gone way up, right? Particularly as you look at the USMCA and Chinese goods coming to Mexico to come to the United States, nakedly circumventing the entire policy goal of imposing tariffs. The goal is to build the iPhone in the United States. The goal is to build manufacturing in the United States. I know that you have never really thought that’s an achievable goal, but that is the goal. That is what the administration promised. We’ve created these trade groups, trade associations, that allow that goal to be circumvented. Do you think the walls are going to keep going up, or do you think they’re going to come back down?I think we’re going to see more pressure to moderate our behavior a little bit because, let’s face it, there are a lot of goods that we, as a country, need access to inexpensive labor. So I’m actually very pro-USMCA as a successor to NAFTA because I actually think there are things that we need inexpensive labor for. Mexico is a good place to source things like that. There are things that we need from Canada.So if we were to look at North America as a trading bloc, then what you would see is the benefits of specialization, which is the whole rationale for trade in the first place. We’re better at doing this, you’re better at doing that; you specialize in that, we’ll specialize in this. We trade; everybody is better off. If you can do that with a community of countries that understand the need for that type of balance, then everybody is better off.I think the problem with China is they’re very happy to have this imbalance, where they want the world to be dependent on them, but they don’t want to buy stuff from the rest of the world. When you have that, then trade doesn’t really work. So I think that’s the problem.I’m hoping we’re going to realize that we’re better off among a group of like-minded countries where we can trade within that bloc. So for example, if the US were to view North American partners and European partners in Japan — and countries in Southeast Asia, Australia, New Zealand, parts of Central and South America, and even Africa — and say, “Okay, let’s trade across this bloc,” then we’d have access to most of what we need, whether it’s critical minerals, low-cost labor, or a lot of technology specialties. We could do much better with that, much better than a go-it-alone strategy in my view.The first part of your book — which I highly recommend the audience read; it’s a fun read — is just setting up the first principles of why we trade at all in the very concept of labor arbitrage. It seems like we’re having a national policy conversation that is 500 steps removed from these basic ideas of why we would trade.It is entirely centered around: can you bring manufacturing back to America because we let all the manufacturing jobs go to Mexico and China, particularly in high tech? And we’re behind. There might be some extraordinarily bad event, like a war, where it’s exposed how little manufacturing capability we have in the United States.That has nothing to do with the basics of specialization in various countries around the world. It’s another problem, and the blunt instrument is, “Boy, it’s bad that all of our drones are made in China. We’re going to prevent drones from being sold here. Of course, our industry will set up drone manufacturing in the United States.” I don’t see that connection. Do you see that working?No. I think that’s a transactional view where you look at one piece at a time as opposed to looking at the bigger picture. I think we have to start with a core principle that the US is a high-cost country. Therefore, if you want manufacturing jobs coming to the US, then you’ve got to have high labor productivity.In fact, if you look at the types of jobs that are coming back to the US, they tend to use a lot of automation, a lot of sophisticated manufacturing processes, and stuff that is high-skill that can justify the high labor cost. Either that, or they are things where we have a technological lead that nobody else knows how to do in the world.I was looking at the high-temperature superalloys that are used in the hot section of jet engines. There are only three companies in the world that know how to cast those, and two of them are in the US, and one of them is in the UK. There are things like that the rest of the world has to buy from us. So if you have high labor productivity or highly differentiated products, those we can make in the US; we can make them successfully. By the way, most of them never left the country.The US, France, and the UK are major suppliers of jet engines to the entire world market. Even the Chinese buy those from the West. So if we have these things that we do better than anybody else, we should invest in those and make sure that we’re always in the lead, and then everybody else will buy from us, and then you’ll have some balance where you can’t be held up.There’s a lot of this thinking like, “I wish I could turn the clock back to the 1980s or the 1970s, when manufacturing was the path to the middle class in the US.” But manufacturing has changed worldwide, and for those jobs that you want to have manufacturing in the US, you’ve got to have high labor productivity or the high differentiation that’ll go with it.I want to stay on the iPhone for one more second. Apple just inked a new deal where they’re going to source a bunch of titanium from a Pennsylvania-based company called Perryman for the iPhone 18 Pro and the new iPhone Duo. They’re going to source that titanium here. They’re then going to ship it to China. They’re going to assemble the phone in China, and they’re going to ship the phones back to us. They do that with Corning and glass as well.I’ve always looked at that. Tim Cook’s job, in particular, is that he’s a statesman. He has to negotiate with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping about iPhone production and tariffs in these supply chains, and the iPhone holds the global economy together. If the price of the iPhone gets too high because of tariffs, maybe there’s an electoral impact in the United States.How do you see products like that? Are they as load-bearing as it feels to me, or are they just examples of the larger system?I think the iPhone is a terrific example of how difficult this problem is. Because right now you have components that have high technological complexity. The iPhone uses the most advanced chips produced by Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company. By the way, most of those chips are still going to be made in Taiwan. TSMC has a fab in Arizona, but its capacity is piddly compared to what it has in Taiwan.Those chips come from one place and require the most sophisticated processing tools that come from ASML in the Netherlands, but also companies like Lam Research and Applied Materials in the US. So it’s that global thing. But the key thing is iPhones also require assembly labor. They require manual assembly because we’re not at the point yet where you can assemble the whole thing with a robot.There’s actually a chapter in my book where I talk about what Henry Ford and the lifestyles of the Chinese Communist Party have to do with assembling iPhones. It turns out it’s a lot. The lifestyles of the Chinese Communist Party have to do with how they mobilize workers in what’s called the Danwei model, which was established after the Communist Revolution. It’s where you have a production site, a walled city with housing for workers, a means of production, warehouses, ways to feed them, and stuff like that.If you ever go to a phone factory in China, the real question is: how do I mobilize 100,000 to 200,000 workers to do this manual assembly on a scale that an Apple needs? They’re trying to do it in India. They’re having some success with India, but that was really hard. Once again, it’s: how do I mobilize manual labor at that level of scale?So the iPhone, as you point out, is a great example of a global product because it needs the highest level of tech, and it also needs the huge workforce to do the manual assembly.There’s actually a great book called Apple in China, which I also recommend. The narrative is that the Chinese government subsidized an awful lot of manufacturing in China. They built these cities, and they built the culture that enables the labor at scale. Your example in the book, again, is LCD factories, where the Chinese government invested in overcapacity, and that drove the price of LCD manufacturing down. Basically, it’s all centered in China now.The flip side of that is, boy, it’s pretty obvious that they stole a bunch of American intellectual property along the way. They developed these manufacturing capabilities. They took a lot of the know-how that Apple imported into that country. They did the same with Tesla in a lot of ways. They stood up an entire electric car industry on the back of the innovation Tesla had started through manufacturing in that country. Now they have those capabilities, and they’re racing ahead of our companies because we don’t actually have the manufacturing know-how.Can you rebalance that? I hear this concern a lot: that you can’t rebalance it. If all the manufacturing happens there, they will actually be state-of-the-art, and we will fall behind.I’m not sure if “stole” is the best description of how they got these capabilities. I would say they learned it, and in many cases we taught it to them. Being a supplier to Apple is often referred to as a golden ticket, and people say, “Well, why is it a golden ticket?” Well, obviously you get cash flow from selling products to them.But the other thing is that Apple is a real taskmaster. By making you work hard to improve your products, improve your specs, meet their performance specs, and meet their cost targets, you get better. The same thing happened when Tesla set up their factory in Shanghai. The fact that they qualified local suppliers raised the game in the Chinese EV market.Another thing I think a lot of people miss about China is that there is actually this very interesting competition going on. Beijing sets policies and objectives, but then all the regional governments, the provinces, and the major cities are competing with each other. They set up this free market dynamic, and so you have this fierce competition between regions.The regions are also very smart about setting objectives. They keep raising the bar for people so the technology gets better. You have a dynamic where there’s really cutthroat competition in the Chinese market, and it’s about survival to make better products at lower prices. That’s something that’s really driving it right now.To your point about how, to the extent we’ve lost the ability to make things, the Chinese have a lot of capabilities. You should walk through some Chinese factories these days. They’re way ahead of the US in terms of using automation, because they’re investing like crazy.I had a student I was talking to about his father’s factory in Shanghai, and he said his father’s answer to everything, every competitive threat, was just more CapEx: “I’m going to throw more capital at it. I’m going to buy the latest machine.” I was in one factory a couple of months ago where the equipment was two or maybe three years old, and they were ripping it out and upgrading it to the latest generation because they said, “This is how we’re going to survive. We have to make the product more efficiently, and we have to make a better product.”So there’s this internal competition in the Chinese marketplace that is really fearsome, and it’s hard for Western companies to compete there, but that is an important dynamic that’s going on as well.The interesting thing about that, as I compare and contrast China with the United States, is that the system in China is understood. It’s stable. You can make a lot of criticisms of that system. I think you can make an endless number of human rights criticisms of the Chinese government. It’s obviously a repressive government in a lot of ways.But the economic system is understood, and it’s controlled at the top in a meaningfully stable way. The goals are apparent, the investment is apparent, and there’s a lot of competition to achieve those goals with that investment.There are two things about that which I think are significant. The first is that China engages in long-term planning, five-year plans. Now, when I was a kid, I used to look at China’s five-year plans, and I thought, “This is a big joke,” because they would make a lot of mistakes, like Mao Zedong’s Great Leap Forward, and they were doing this new type of tillage in farming, and they caused this huge famine and millions of people died.But to the credit of the government there, when they do this type of long-range planning, they learn from their mistakes, and they get better. If you look at their current five-year plans and the last couple of five-year plans, they’re good plans. They understand what’s important, and they focus on those things that are important.Then the second point is about what kinds of people they have implementing these plans. I was in one of these third-tier cities some number of years ago, and I was having dinner with the economic development commission there. At the beginning of dinner, I said, “Hey guys, just for fun, let’s go around the table and talk about what you studied in school.” It was mechanical engineering, industrial engineering, electrical engineering, metallurgy, metallurgy, mechanical engineering. You go to Washington and ask what people studied in school, and it’s political science, economics, and government.So you have these technocrats competing in technology-intensive businesses and having that understanding. By the way, that’s one of the reasons I wrote this book: I was serving on these committees appointed by the Commerce Secretary on supply chains, and I realized we have civil servants who don’t have the exposure to supply chains and how stuff is actually made.China had this plan that was called the 863 plan. The 863 plan was when four scholars went to the government in Beijing in March of 1986 — that’s why it’s called “863”; it was ‘86, March. I remember the first time I looked at the 863 plan, and it was, “If we want to be a modern economy, we have to be good at these things.”I looked at that plan in the 1990s, and I said, “This is a good plan.” And they’ve executed every one of those things. They said, “We need to be good at all these things, like information technology, biotechnology.” In semiconductors, they still have a way to go, but they identified civil aircraft. But they identified all these different technologies like communications technology, software, and robotics.I would contrast that with the Trump administration here in Trump’s second term, where… We already talked about Liberation Day. Howard Lutnick is on television saying, “We’re going to move manufacturing back to the United States. This is the goal of the tariffs.”Three weeks later, there are 900 lawsuits about the tariffs, and Howard Lutnick is back on TV saying, “Robots will do all the manufacturing now. This is the goal. We’re going to do heavy automation.” And then the tariffs get struck down, and they find a new law for different tariffs.It does not seem like the same long-term planning that can be stuck to, or the same environment where businesses understand the stability of the trading system such that they can compete ferociously. Every CEO who does manufacturing and comes on the show usually ends up talking to me about how they scrambled to buy RAM at affordable prices to make their products, which has to keep them from doing anything else.How would you contrast that? Can we get out of this moment where it’s a pure scramble, or is this fully shaking everything up?We’re in a very transactional environment. Everything is short-term, and these rapid changes that you see in the tariffs... If you look at a map of 2025 and 2026 and put a dot everywhere there was some tariff action, it looks like a shotgun hit the wall. There are all these spots all over the place.The problem with that is when you have that type of instability, it’s very hard for a company to make any long-term plans. Before I build a factory, I want to know that I’m going to have stable demand for a couple of years, at least until I have a chance of earning a return on that thing. I’ve talked to a couple of companies about this. These were overseas companies thinking about coming into the US market, and they said, “Well, I can’t do it because things keep changing. Do I go to Mexico? Do I go to the US? What part of the US do I go into?”Especially with things like semiconductor fabs, you need to know that you’re going to be able to get 10 to 20 years out of it. When things change every couple of weeks, what that does instead is say, “I’m just going to hold off on an investment because it’s just too uncertain. It changes too often.”Are you seeing that slow down in investment? Are you seeing companies say, “We can’t actually invest in manufacturing in the United States”?It varies. I see that with a lot of companies asking, “Where do I want to put my production operations?” Okay, now we see some things like car plants coming into the US, and usually that’s a function of the pain being too great.But the whole auto tariff thing is also a little bit crazy. If you look historically at production strategies in the auto industry, typically when you build a plant, you size it to build about 200,000 to 250,000 units of a model or a model family, because that’s like the efficient scale for an auto plant.Then what you have is a company like BMW that says, “Great, I’m going to build all my X Series SUVs in South Carolina. I’ll build the 3 Series somewhere else. I’ll build the 5 Series somewhere else, and I’ll build the 7 Series somewhere else. And then what I’ll do is exchange them.”So BMW in South Carolina or Mercedes in Alabama, they build certain models in the US, export them to the rest of the world, and then import other models so that you have the whole product line. Toyota does that. For example, they build more Camrys in the US than anywhere else, and they were exporting some of those as well.But then when you start putting tariffs on imports, that screws up that whole strategy. Again, it’s a decision that was made without understanding how the automakers had laid out that strategy.. You need to understand how the supply chain is structured and why it’s structured the way it is, and then you can be more thoughtful..Do you see tariffs as mostly protectionist? I was in France earlier this year, and I took an Uber, and I think it was a BYD Seal, a Chinese EV. I asked the French Uber driver, “How do you like this car?” He was very French, and he literally did the thing. He goes, “Peugeot is shit.” I almost started clapping because it was amazing. He’s like, “If the French government would just allow the Chinese government to sell these cars here, these companies would all be dead.”In the United States, I think Jim Farley, the CEO of Ford, is running around saying the Chinese EVs are superior to American products. It’s the tariffs that protect our markets and protect our manufacturers, because you could import the cars, but you’d pay such high tariffs that they’re economically infeasible.That’s just pure protectionism. That goes against what you’re saying, which is that you need to protect your industry until their products are good enough to compete on the global scale. But we’re not doing that with our carmakers. We’re just protecting them.Yeah, and there’s a cost associated with that. So, for example, one of the famous tariffs is a so-called chicken tax. I talk about this in the book as well. The chicken tax resulted from this trade spat where we put tariffs on imported light trucks.SUVs are built on that platform. It’s one of the reasons the Detroit automakers have focused on SUVs and light trucks. That’s their profit center because there’ve been tariffs on that, and it’s only happened in the last decade or so that Toyota and Nissan and others have made more light trucks in the US and Mexico. So that’s one of the results of that type of tariff distortion.Wait. But that’s a policy victory, right? Toyota, Nissan, and all the other foreign manufacturers are going to make trucks in the United States. You’ve gotten some economic benefit; they can compete, and maybe all the trucks are going to get better.You get some economic benefit, but one of the reasons the Detroit guys still make so many trucks and SUVs on those platforms is because they’re more profitable, which says the price is higher than it might otherwise have been. But I do see the benefit of that.Although I have to say, I was walking around the Toyota factory in Georgetown, Kentucky. I’m walking around with the plant manager, and I said, “You’re making sedans here?” He said, “Yep,” and a lot of the Detroit guys have given up making sedans because they can’t make any money. I said, “And you’re using parts that mostly come from Kentucky, Ohio, Indiana, Alabama, Mississippi, and Texas, and some from Mexico and Japan, but mostly domestic content.” He’s like, “Yep.” I said, “And you’re using American workers.” He said, “Yep.” I said, “You’re using American-made steel.”I’m trying to get out of him that, okay, look, I know American steel costs a lot more than imported steel because I’ve been in other factories that are still importing steel despite the steel tariffs because they say it’s still cheaper in Asia. But I said, “You’re using American-made steel.” So I’m trying to get that out of him: how much he’s paying for steel.Obviously, he’s not going to tell me, but he does say, “We have a strategic long-term relationship with our supplier.” That tells you a lot, which is that there are ways you can do these things. You have to work with your suppliers. You have to give them longer-term arrangements, be less transactional, more strategic on things like that. So I think you can do it, but it really takes a comprehensive and more thoughtful approach.I understand the rationale for putting tariffs on foreign goods that undercut our markets. You’re just going to increase the cost, and then maybe the consumer will buy the domestic product, and that’s better for our economy. It just hasn’t seemed to have worked.I don’t see Liberation Day as having done anything except generally raise prices on everything. We haven’t actually remapped the global economy. And a lot of what you’re describing is, well, the system is pretty resilient. The system was pretty resilient to COVID. The system was pretty resilient to an oil tanker getting stuck in the Suez Canal. The system has been pretty resilient to the war in Iran. The system has been pretty resilient to absolutely chaotic tariffs.Maybe some prices have risen, and I’m sure we’re going to get listeners pointing out that all the prices have risen. It feels like the only thing the system isn’t resilient to is the AI industry wanting every scrap of RAM that the whole world can produce. And so now there’s not going to be inexpensive cell phones.What will push the system over the breaking point? Because globalization has seemed generally resilient to a bunch of people who want it to be over.I think what you’re highlighting is that it’s really the power of the market. In the case of closing the Strait of Hormuz, Brent North Sea crude prices didn’t go to $150 a barrel like I was afraid they would, and a lot of people were afraid they would because the market adjusted.We applied a lot of tariffs on Liberation Day. The first response was circumvention or front-running. The next response was tariff engineering. The next response is like, “Okay, let me move production to Vietnam or let me move production to Mexico, and I’ll find a way around that.” Now, eventually, when you close down all those things, then prices eventually have to rise.In the case of memory chips, that’s a different problem because the demand far outstripped the capacity. I used to always buy memory cards on Black Friday. Forget that this year.Yeah, it’s all over.I’m just glad I stocked up on a previous Black Friday.If you want to know my prediction for when the AI industry will meet its true political end, it’s when Grand Theft Auto VI comes out. Everyone goes out to buy a PS5, and they realize it’s more expensive now at the end of its life cycle than it was at the beginning because the price of memory has skyrocketed.Yeah, no kidding. We’re talking about huge amounts. But that’s the same thing. We’re in a phase where we see all these tactical actions taken by the government, very transactional, without necessarily understanding all the complex interconnections and interdependencies.You may have noticed, for example, that the administration temporarily suspended the Jones Act. I don’t know if you remember that. Why did they temporarily suspend the Jones Act? Because oil refineries on the East Coast of the US couldn’t get their oil from Texas cheaply because there were no domestic supertankers.The Jones Act requires that if you move stuff from Texas to New Jersey, you have to have a US-owned, US-crewed, US-built, very large crude carrier. There aren’t any because we don’t build those in the US. So that’s why it’s cheaper to bring oil from Algeria to New Jersey than it is to bring it from Texas. And that’s why they suspended the Jones Act for a while. At least they understood that.I know at least some of our audience is going to be listening to this conversation, and you’re steeped in global trade. You wrote a book to educate our government about how it works from the basics, which I think is sorely needed.But a lot of the promise for young people in our politics lately is that we will rebuild American capacity. We will rebuild manufacturing capacity. We will bring back a bunch of jobs where you don’t need an advanced degree in AI prompt engineering or whatever to see the future. We will bring back the dignity of work.Politicians on both sides are making these promises all the time, and a lot of that requires closing down trade, forcing that economic activity back within our borders. It just seems like that isn’t likely. So I’m not going to ask you whether or not that is totally likely. I’m going to ask: what’s more likely instead?Well, I think what’s more likely is that we will see efforts as you describe. I would love to sit down with people and say, okay, we want to move this type of production back to the US. Let’s take a more strategic, more nuanced approach, understanding the bigger picture, considering what levers are available.The US is still a big, attractive market. It is the largest market in the world. It is the most attractive market in the world. That’s, by the way, why the Chinese all want to come here: because they can make some money here that they can’t make elsewhere. So then how do we harness that market power and that market pull with a more nuanced understanding of why our supply chains are organized the way they are today? Recognizing that, can I build a strategy to bring important things that are very strategic for the US to know how to do?Let’s think about how we fix this problem with an understanding of that bigger picture.Willy, it’s been great to talk to you. It is always just a pleasure. We have to have you back faster than five years. Thank you so much for being on Decoder.Thanks for having me.Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email!Decoder with Nilay PatelA podcast from The Verge about big ideas and other problems.SUBSCRIBE NOW!
items.author: Nilay Patel
items.titleZh: AI热潮背后隐藏的供应链成本
items.descriptionZh:
这是一场围绕全球供应链未来走向的深度访谈。主持人Nilay Patel与哈佛商学院管理实践教授、经济学家Willy Shih展开对话，后者刚刚出版新书《我的东西从哪来？全球供应链背后的强大经济学》。访谈背景设定在一个全球化遭遇多重压力的时刻：特朗普政府关税政策反复变动、制造业回流承诺大多落空、AI基础设施竞赛吞噬全球计算资源，而政界关于"全球化是否正在终结"的争论愈演愈烈。Shih的核心论点是：全球供应链的形态归根结底由经济学力量驱动，政治意志若无视这一底层逻辑，其政策目标往往会被市场以各种方式规避或扭曲。

Shih首先回顾了他准确预判富士康威斯康星州LCD工厂项目失败的经历。他从第一性原理出发，指出当地缺乏支撑面板工厂所需的玻璃基板供应商和足够的结构钢材与混凝土用量，而面板制造对厂房稳定性有极高要求。这一案例成为他分析供应链问题的典型方法：不只看组装环节，而要追溯整个配套生态。

关于全球化的基本原理，Shih强调劳动力套利和专业化分工是贸易的根本驱动力。他以冷冻鱼从阿拉斯加运到中国青岛加工再运回、腰果在越南加工等看似反常的贸易路线为例，说明这些都是成本最优的经济选择。当美国对中国商品加征关税后，市场的第一反应是规避——2025年第一季度美国从爱尔兰进口创历史纪录，随后半年进口骤降，正是企业提前囤货的结果；同时，中国至墨西哥之间新开通多条直达海运集装箱航线，实质是将零部件运至墨西哥组装，再以《美墨加协定》框架免税进入美国市场，直接绕开关税壁垒。

在贸易失衡问题上，Shih指出中国持续运行巨额贸易顺差，实际上是将自身经济问题出口到美国，以牺牲他国就业为代价。欧洲尤其是德国已开始意识到汽车产业面临的生存危机。他认为，理想的解决方案是构建一个以北美为核心、联合欧洲、日本、东南亚、澳大利亚、新西兰及部分中南美洲和非洲国家的"志同道合贸易集团"，在集团内实现专业化分工，同时确保关键矿产、低成本劳动力和技术专长的可获得性，这比单打独斗策略更优。

访谈深入对比了中美制造业生态。Shih指出，中国制造业优势并非简单来自"窃取"技术，更多是"学习"——苹果和特斯拉等企业为满足自身严苛的规格、性能和成本要求，实际上倒逼中国供应商大幅提升了制造能力。他特别强调三个被忽视的维度：其一，中国从五年规划到1986年"863计划"的长远规划能力，虽早期犯过重大错误，但持续从错误中学习，规划质量显著提升；其二，中国地方政府之间形成激烈竞争格局，各省市相互比拼产业目标，制造出类似自由市场的残酷竞争动态；其三，中国负责产业规划的经济官员多为机械、电气、冶金等工科背景，而美国华盛顿的相关官员多出身政治学、经济学和法学，缺乏对制造流程的实际认知。此外，中国工厂在自动化投资上极为激进，两三年即淘汰设备升级换代，以"更多资本开支"应对一切竞争威胁。

以iPhone为例，Shih展示了全球最复杂消费品的供应链全貌：最先进的芯片来自台积电台湾厂（亚利桑那工厂产能与之相比微不足道），制造芯片所需的高端设备来自荷兰ASML以及美国Lam Research和Applied Materials；钛金属从宾夕法尼亚州Perryman公司采购后运往中国，最终整机在中国完成组装。组装环节仍需大量人工，中国通过继承自革命时期的"单位"模式，能够动员十万至二十万工人在封闭园区内实现规模化手工装配，印度正在尝试复制但难度极大。Shih认为iPhone是理解供应链问题难度的绝佳样本：它同时依赖最高端技术和最庞大的劳动力动员能力。

关于制造业回流，Shih直言美国是高成本国家，回流的制造业岗位必须具备高劳动生产率或高度差异化。他以喷气发动机热端高温合金为例，全球仅三家公司掌握铸造技术，两家在美国、一家在英国，这类高壁垒产品才是美国制造业的合理定位。他批评当前关税政策的交易性和不稳定性：2025至2026年间关税行动散布如"霰弹枪打墙"，企业无法做出十年至二十年回收期的长期投资决策，半导体厂和汽车厂选址尤为受制。汽车行业原本的全球分工策略——宝马在南卡罗来纳生产X系列出口全球、同时进口其他系列——也被关税打乱。他提到"鸡肉税"的历史案例，说明对轻型卡车的关税扭曲了底特律车企的产品结构，使其长期依赖高利润SUV和皮卡，消费者为此支付更高价格。

在系统韧性方面，Shih认为市场调整能力极强：霍尔木兹海峡危机未使布伦特原油飙升至每桶150美元，苏伊士运河堵塞和新冠冲击均被消化。但当前真正的稀缺瓶颈是AI产业对内存芯片的吞噬性需求，叠加关税层层收紧后价格终将上行。主持人调侃称，等到《侠盗猎车手VI》发售时玩家发现PS5因内存涨价而更贵，可能就是AI产业触及政治临界点的时刻。Shih还提到政府曾临时暂停《琼斯法案》以缓解东海岸炼油厂无法廉价获取德州原油的问题，恰恰说明决策者偶尔也能理解供应链互联性。

最后，Shih呼吁采取更具战略性和精细化的产业政策：美国仍是全球最大、最具吸引力的市场，这正是中国企业希望进入的原因；应利用这一市场引力，在理解供应链现有结构的基础上，有针对性地将真正具有战略意义的能力留在或引回国内，而非依赖粗糙的关税工具。他指出，政治人物关于恢复制造业尊严和就业的承诺需要更细致的产业理解来支撑，否则政策效果可能适得其反。

items.description:

items.content: After partnering with Moises earlier this year, SoundCloud is now adding integration with another AI music platform, ElevenLabs. Now, rather than having to export and download your outputs from ElevenLabs and then upload them to SoundCloud, you can publish them directly. As part of the partnership, SoundCloud Artist Pro subscribers are also getting three months of ElevenMusic Pro for free, so they can experiment with generative AI and potentially alienate their fans. Songs published from ElevenLabs directly to SoundCloud will be labeled as such, making clear their AI origins.The integration between SoundCloud and ElevenLabs isn’t as deep as the Moises integration. That lets users pull tracks from SoundCloud into Moises for stem separation and remixing, then republish them directly to SoundCloud.In general, SoundCloud has seemed more willing to embrace AI-generated music than other streaming services. While it “encourages” users subject to EU rules to label tracks as “AI-generated or manipulated” and has rules against impersonation, it’s also partnered with multiple generative AI music platforms. SoundCloud has also avoided the loud-and-proud press releases detailing how many spammy AI songs it’s removed from its platform, or bragging about demonetizing them.
items.author: Terrence O’Brien
items.titleZh: 你可以直接从 ElevenLabs 将 AI 音乐发布到 SoundCloud
items.descriptionZh:
SoundCloud 正在扩大对 AI 生成音乐的支持。继今年早些时候与 AI 音乐平台 Moises 合作后，SoundCloud 又与另一家 AI 音乐平台 ElevenLabs 达成集成。此前，用户需要先从 ElevenLabs 导出并下载生成结果，再上传到 SoundCloud；现在，用户可以将 ElevenLabs 的输出直接发布到 SoundCloud。作为合作的一部分，SoundCloud Artist Pro 订阅用户还可免费获得三个月 ElevenMusic Pro，用于试验生成式 AI 音乐创作，尽管这也可能让部分粉丝感到不适。凡是从 ElevenLabs 直接发布到 SoundCloud 的歌曲都会被明确标注，以说明其 AI 来源。

从技术集成深度看，SoundCloud 与 ElevenLabs 的合作不如与 Moises 的集成深入。Moises 集成允许用户将 SoundCloud 上的曲目拉入 Moises，进行分轨分离和混音，然后再直接重新发布回 SoundCloud；而与 ElevenLabs 的集成目前主要解决的是 AI 生成音乐从创作平台到分发平台的一键发布问题，减少导出、下载、上传等中间环节。新闻未披露具体的性能参数或量化对比数据，核心差异体现在工作流简化程度和平台间集成深度上。

整体来看，SoundCloud 相比其他流媒体服务更愿意接纳 AI 生成音乐。平台一方面“鼓励”受欧盟规则约束的用户将曲目标注为“AI 生成或被操纵”，并制定了禁止冒充他人的规则；另一方面已与多个生成式 AI 音乐平台建立合作。与一些高调宣传删除垃圾 AI 歌曲或取消其变现资格的平台不同，SoundCloud 并未大张旗鼓地发布此类治理数据。此次集成的影响在于：AI 音乐创作者可以更便捷地在 SoundCloud 发布和实验作品，平台通过来源标注提升透明度，但 AI 音乐大量涌入也可能带来内容质量、粉丝接受度和平台治理方面的挑战。应用场景主要覆盖 AI 音乐创作、生成式音乐实验、分轨混音再发布以及订阅捆绑试用等。

items.title: Intel leaker claims Nova Lake desktop chips have 5.1 GHz clock limit beyond 90°C
items.description: A known Intel leaker claims that Intel's next-generation processors will top out at 5.1 GHz if the CPU core temperatures aren't kept below 90°C.
items.content: Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 7 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter According to new information from reasonably reliable Intel leaker Jaykihn, Intel's upcoming Nova Lake desktop CPUs will have an unusual limiter applied. He claims that the next-gen desktop parts from Intel will "universally limit the maximum core frequency to 5.1 GHz when above 90°C." That doesn't mean the parts will top out at 5.1 GHz, which would be disastrous, but it does mean that you're going to need some darn good cooling to reach high clock rates on Nova Lake desktop CPUs.Go deeper with TH Premium: CPU (Image credit: Tom's Hardware)Intel VP Robert Hallock sets Nova Lake expectations, teases return to Raptor Lake for DDR4 platformsCPU scaling with DLSSIntel's one-two punch plan in desktop CPUs is taking shapeBenchmarking AMD's BC-250, offering Steam Machine-like performance at half the priceAMD splits Zen 7 into three EPYC families for 2028 and starts selling server CPUs by the agent Let's be clear about what he's saying. He's not saying that Nova Lake CPUs can't go above 5.1 GHz. He's also not saying that Nova Lake CPUs have their thermal limit at 90°C. While Jaykihn doesn't provide any clock rate information, he does imply that the chips will go above that, possibly quite significantly, as long as the thermals are kept in check, and he does say that the "Tjmax" value of Nova Lake is 100°C. Notably, that's a drop from 105°C in Arrow Lake, although prior-gen Raptor Lake CPUs had the same 100°C peak.Preliminary. Nova Lake -S desktop processors will universally limit the maximum core frequency to 5.1GHz when above 90C. This is separate behavior from traditional TJMax thermal throttling at 100C. Alike TJMax, this temperature threshold cannot be shifted upwards.November 4, 2026The mechanism that this most clearly resembles is Intel's own Thermal Velocity Boost. TVB, if you're not familiar, is the feature that allows high-end Intel CPUs to hit their highest clock rates. Put simply, TVB simply says that if the chip isn't overheating, it can go 100-300 MHz higher than its rated Turbo Boost Max speed. It's a little confusing, because these TVB clock rates are often quoted as the "Max Turbo Frequency"; Intel even does this itself. But TVB clocks are not the same as standard turbo clocks, and a lot of users who don't have exotic cooling probably never actually see these speeds in practice since they do require optimal conditions.Latest Videos FromTom's HardwareWatch full video here: Does this mean that the practical limit of Nova Lake desktop CPU clocks is 5.1 GHz? Well, that depends on how hard these parts are to cool. Remember, we're dealing with chips fabricated on a 2nm-class process; in this case, it's reportedly TSMC's N2P for the compute tiles, while the peripheral chiplets are all on Intel's own 18A or 18A-P. This has consequences, as N2P is reportedly much denser than 18A, but it also lacks back-side power delivery, which means that the thermal resistance of the individual dies is considerably lower. Combined with much lower power consumption from a real node step, it may turn out that Nova Lake is actually quite easy to keep cool.Ultimately, that is going to depend in part on how much Intel decides to push the "fMax", or maximum frequency. Rumors have put AMD's Zen 6 desktop Ryzen processors above 6 GHz for peak clock rates; if that's true, Intel could be looking at as much as a 20% clock rate disadvantage at 5.1 GHz. Obviously, as noted above, the chips are expected to have a higher fMax than that, but it remains to be seen how easily users can keep the parts cool enough to make use of the extra clock rate headroom given this new limit. Both Intel's flagship Core Ultra 9 285K and the Red Team's extant Zen 5-based Ryzen 9 9950X can reach 5.7 GHz before overclocking. You may like Leaked Intel Nova Lake product list has three 'BFC' chips with up to 144MB of game-boosting L3 cache Intel's Core Ultra 400 'Nova Lake' launch schedule leaks out Intel confirms Nova Lake CPUs will use advanced 18A-P node, more details at CES Intel's familiar eXtreme Tuning Utility (XTU) software gives users full control over TVB, Tjmax, and core turbo ratios. (Image credit: Future)For tuners, a frustrating detail is that this 5.1 GHz hard clock limit apparently "cannot be raised." That means folks doing system tuning on Nova Lake will be strongly encouraged to undervolt to reduce the thermal output of their processors and help them maintain high performance. That's unusual, as historically Intel allows users to adjust the thermal throttle point of their processors when overclocking. That may potentially still be the case on processors unlocked for overclocking, of course; Jaykihn is reporting based on leaks and engineering samples rather than final released products.Even if Nova Lake doesn't scale clocks much over Arrow Lake, it could still be quite a bit faster than the previous generation. Recall that the new chips will come with new core architectures and new technologies, including APX core extensions and bLLC, Intel's long-awaited response to AMD's 3D V-Cache. Forecasts are indicating that gaming performance could be as much as 33% faster than Arrow Lake, which would be huge. However, this 5.1 GHz limit could be a downer for people who are interested in the rumored 52-core version of Nova Lake. We'll find out how much it matters when the Core Ultra 4000 series launches either very late this year or very early next year, although we wouldn't expect the 52-core flagship or bLLC versions until next summer.Stay On the Cutting Edge: Get the Tom's Hardware NewsletterGet Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.Contact me with news and offers from other Future brandsReceive email from us on behalf of our trusted partners or sponsors Follow Tom's Hardware on Google News, or add us as a preferred source, to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds.
